CREATE AN ACCOUNT SIGN IN AI Magazine Interview How Wikipedia’s Editors Keep the Online Encyclopedia Human-Written AI-generated text is harder to spot, but that hasn’t deterred them Eliza Strickland 21 Oct 2026 4 min read Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor. She also covers AI and biomedical engineering. Ellia Lebleu is a cofounder of the WikiProject AI Cleanup effort to keep Wikipedia human-written. Stuart Bradford Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup , a volunteer effort launched in 2023 to find and remove AI-generated material from Wikipedia that breaks the website’s guidelines. When the cleanup began, AI writing was often betrayed by conspicuous clichés. Today, the project’s volunteers are developing tools to detect subtler forms of machine-generated content and debating AI’s role in the world’s most widely used encyclopedia. When did you realize Wikipedia had a problem with AI-generated material? Ellia Lebleu: It was around December 2023. A few other editors and I were chatting on Wikipedia’s Discord server, and we had all seen very strange articles with the same odd characteristics. They repeated phrases like “stands as a testament” or “rich cultural heritage.” They sometimes had conclusion sections, or sections called “Why is this important?” That was very typical of ChatGPT in 2023 and early 2024 but very odd for Wikipedia articles—and very easy to spot. Then I decided, let’s create an official project on Wikipedia so more people can deal with this. Ellia Lebleu Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes , part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology. How do editors spot AI-generated writing today? Lebleu: By 2025, the signs of AI writing were becoming subtler and more structural. For example, AI loves the “rule of three,” negative parallelisms, and other structures of speech that aren’t conclusive by themselves but become meaningful as they accumulate. We also look beyond the article. If someone writes five articles of thousands of words each in 5 minutes, there is reason to suspect AI. Does the AI problem just appear in the main text, or also in citations? Lebleu: Fake or misleading citations have become a major worry. Sometimes an AI hallucinates a citation entirely, although that’s much rarer today because of retrieval-augmented generation that allows the AI to find sources. More often, it finds a real source but gets its content completely wrong. AI citations that don’t actually support what is being written are extremely commonplace. English Wikipedia recently prohibited editors from using LLMs to generate articles. How much AI-generated content is still getting through? Lebleu: I’ve been working with [AI-detection company] Pangram to estimate the proportion of AI-generated content. I tested it on Wikipedia content from before ChatGPT and found no false positives, so its results provide a very conservative lower bound. In late 2025, it flagged perhaps 20 percent of new articles and drafts as AI-generated. In early 2026, that went down to 15 or 16 percent. But we don’t yet know whether that’s because our recent policies have had an effect or because models are getting more powerful and Pangram hasn’t had time to adapt. Is Wikipedia using AI to combat AI? Lebleu: Another Wikipedia editor has made an AI source verifier, which goes through the sources on a page and checks whether they match the claims. Since it is itself an AI model, there is no guarantee that it will be correct every time. But if you want something that works at scale and filters out obvious cases, it’s a good first step. The Wikimedia Foundation is also working on a tool called Paste Check , which can flag text pasted directly from some AI chatbots . And we’ve seen Claude sometimes say, “I can’t write a Wikipedia article; it would go against Wikipedia’s policies.” If all major AI companies implemented that kind of prompt refusal, it wouldn’t solve the problem entirely, because there are still open-weight models that can be tweaked to avoid restrictions. But it would help with people who use commercial models and aren’t especially familiar with the technology. Can you tell if the rule prohibiting AI writing is working? Lebleu: It’s still a little early to tell. We see possible effects, such as prompt refusal and the apparent slight drop in AI-generated content. But again, we don’t yet know if that is because models are getting better or because beginners are learning the rules. The vast majority of AI-generated content is submitted by beginner editors, so we’ve made many efforts to make the rule very visible in welcome messages, editing help, and advice. What if AI becomes capable of writing truly reliable Wikipedia articles? Lebleu: That’s one of the big questions we’re facing. When the guideline was passed, it was for very practical reasons: We were flooded with AI content, we didn’t have good tools, and we needed to put a stop to it. But since then, it has taken on a more philosophical dimension. Many people have called Wikipedia “the last good place on the internet.” Being a place that was, in theory, free from AI slop has become part of Wikipedia’s identity. A lot of Wikipedia’s communication is now centered on the idea that we’re a human-written encyclopedia. Even AI companies find that interesting. It can be valuable to have a purely human-written corpus on which to [train] AI systems. The fact that Wikipedia is still that, and will remain that for at least the near future, makes it a precious resource that isn’t replicated anywhere else. But will the people who read and contribute to Wikipedia want it to become partially AI-generated if that makes it more comprehensive? We could preserve Wikipedia’s identity as a human-written corpus while also offering an AI-assisted option. Has Wikipedia reckoned with the idea of “Google Zero”—a possible future in which websites no longer get traffic from Google search? Lebleu: If everything goes through AI search and websites plummet to zero visibility, how do we expose Wikipedia and show that it can be edited and that people can still contribute? Wikipedia is frequently cited in [Google’s] AI Overviews, but users may only see an AI answer citing Wikipedia. They may not realize that Wikipedia is a living project they can edit and contribute to. The Wikimedia Foundation is working on an attribution framework that could give AI users more information about the article [being cited]: when it was last edited, how comprehensive it is, whether editors have flagged problems, and perhaps even a call to action. In the future, readers might even contribute through AI models : “The AI cited Wikipedia, but there seems to be an error. Can I make an edit request and add this other source I found?” I can see a very strong symbiotic relationship between Wikipedia and AI models in the future. I don’t see Wikipedia disappearing, but I can see it taking a very different shape. Yesterday, AI was something to clean up. Today, it’s a tool to help us with the cleanup. Tomorrow, it will be the air we breathe. title: US Government is hiding a secret court ruling about how it spies on Americans
body_text: The US Government Is Hiding a Secret Court Ruling About How It Spies on Americans | WIRED Skip to main content THE WIRED APP IS HERE DOWNLOAD NOW » Menu WIRED SECURITY POLITICS THE BIG STORY BUSINESS SCIENCE CULTURE REVIEWS Menu WIRED Account Account Newsletters Security Politics The Big Story Business Science Culture Reviews Chevron More Expand The Big Interview Magazine Events WIRED Insider WIRED Consulting Newsletters Podcasts Video Livestreams WIRED Store Search Search Dell Cameron Security Oct 26, 2026 10:09 AM The US Government Is Hiding a Secret Court Ruling About How It Spies on Americans Two US senators say the Trump administration is breaking the law by withholding the FISA court decision while it presses Congress to renew America’s most sweeping surveillance program. Photo-Illustration: Jobanny Cabrera; Getty Images Comment Loader Save Story Save this story Comment Loader Save Story Save this story Two Democratic senators who have long overseen US intelligence say the Trump administration is illegally withholding a secret court’s findings from Congress until lawmakers renew a program that lets federal agents read Americans’ communications without a warrant. Seven months ago, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court objected to search filters that let intelligence analysts pull Americans’ messages from intercepted data without the approvals, written justifications, or records the law requires. The court approved another year of surveillance anyway. The ruling has never been made public, and Senators Ron Wyden of Oregon and Adam Schiff of California say the administration’s own deadline for releasing it passed in September. The program, Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), lapsed in June after Congress failed to renew it, though collection continues under the court’s March approval. The administration’s own public documentation says rulings like this one are reviewed for public release “within 180 days of issuance.” That window closed September 13, even as intelligence officials press lawmakers to reauthorize the program by the end of the year. Wyden, the longest-serving member of the Senate Intelligence Committee, and Schiff, the former chair of its House counterpart, say the administration owes Congress an explanation for the delay, and the names of the officials responsible, by November 6. “If this administration won’t follow this simple statutory directive,” the senators told Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Attorney General Todd Blanche in a demand letter obtained exclusively by WIRED , “it is unclear why Congress or the American people should trust this administration to follow any of the other legal limits to Section 702.” Outside Congress, Demand Progress and 22 other civil liberties and government accountability groups on Monday urged congressional leaders to refuse to reauthorize Section 702 “while the administration actively withholds legally mandated information about how the surveillance program operates.” Signatories range from the American Civil Liberties Union to the conservative-backed Project for Privacy and Surveillance Accountability. The Trump administration has already been pressed, and has promised, to release the ruling. In April, senators Tom Cotton and Mark Warner, the Intelligence Committee’s Republican chair and Democratic vice chair, pressed the administration to release it within 15 days so it could inform the Senate’s debate. In July, asked in writing whether he would commit to declassifying it by the 180-day deadline, Blanche replied, “Yes.” Warner “has been clear that he supports transparency with regard to Section 702,” his communications director, Rachel Cohen, tells WIRED. Neither former director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard nor Bill Pulte, who briefly replaced her as acting director, “were responsive,” Cohen says, “but Senator Warner expects that DNI Clayton will declassify the opinion, consistent with the bipartisan letter and as required by law.” Cotton’s office did not respond to a request for comment. The White House, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, and the US Justice Department did not answer questions WIRED sent Friday about the delay. Clayton, who is legally responsible as director of national intelligence for declassifying the ruling, has made no such promise. Asked before his July confirmation whether he would ensure the opinion was public before Congress voted on reauthorization, he wrote only that the government was “working arduously to expeditiously declassify” it and had made the full opinion available to lawmakers. Some of what the court found is already known. A FISA court opinion declassified last year described a similar FBI tool, a “participants filter” that let agents select people in contact with surveillance targets and read their messages. In February 2025, the Justice Department’s National Security Division told the court the tool had been running searches no one counted. The FBI shut it off the next month and switched it back on later that year , after the department approved a rebuilt version. This year’s ruling went beyond that. The court found that tools agencies use to narrow intercepted data to an American’s messages amount to searches of Americans, subject to the same limits, and ordered them rebuilt, The New York Times reported in April , citing unclassified administration talking points sent to lawmakers. Senator Alex Padilla said in a written question to Blanche that the Justice Department “is appealing portions” of the ruling “limiting the government’s use of certain filtering tools.” While the ruling stayed secret, seven intelligence agency fact sheets from March 2026, one dated the day of the ruling , cited a 98.9 percent compliance rate for FBI searches of Americans and credited Section 702 with stopping a planned terrorist attack on a Taylor Swift concert in Vienna . None mentions the court’s findings. The figure appears nowhere in the Justice Department inspector general’s October 2025 review of those searches, which put the compliance rate at 98.6 percent and could not conclude that “the FBI’s querying compliance issues are entirely in the past.” According to the fact sheets, FBI auditors review every such search. FBI director Kash Patel closed the bureau’s Office of Internal Auditing last May and moved its auditors into another division. The bureau’s search counts before 2025 also omit queries run through the participants filter, searches the government’s own privacy watchdog says are “ not possible to track .” Lawmakers who have read the ruling hint that it says more. Senator Dick Durbin, the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, urged colleagues on the Senate floor in June to read it in a secure room. “I have seen it,” he said. Once they did, he told them, “your opinion of the role of FISA and the rights of Americans will be impacted for sure.” Wyden has also warned about a classified interpretation of Section 702 that he says multiple administrations have relied on and refused to declassify. “When it is eventually declassified,” he said in March , “the American people are going to be stunned that it took so long and that Congress had been debating this authority with insufficient information.” The Trump administration has until November 6 to answer the senators. The court’s current approval of the program expires in March. Surveillance reform advocates say the administration may try to avoid that fight by attaching a renewal to the annual defense authorization bill, which Congress usually finalizes in December. In 2023, lawmakers extended Section 702 for four months through that year’s defense bill after a Senate effort to strip the provision failed. This year’s House and Senate versions of the bill do not yet include it. title: Anthropic trained Claude on illegally obtained Stanford professors' books
body_text: Anthropic illegally trained Claude with Stanford professors’ books Search Search Remove Ads Subscribe to Digest Log in News • Campus Life Anthropic illegally trained Claude with Stanford professors’ books Anthropic illegally trained Claude on books from Stanford professors (Photo: JACK BERNARDO/The Stanford Daily) By April Yu Published Oct. 27, 2026, 2:46 a.m., last updated Oct. 27, 2026, 3:19 a.m. AI giant Anthropic illegally scraped and pirated the work of over 10 Stanford professors to train its Claude models, a federal judge ruled in a May 2026 lawsuit. Anthropic previously trained Claude on illegally obtained texts from professors Tobias Wolff, Abraham Verghese, Chang-Rae Lee, Daniel Mason, Hayagreeva Rao and Myra Strober. In Bartz v. Anthropic, which the Authors Alliance calls the largest copyright settlement involving an AI company, Judge William Alsup ruled that Anthropic could no longer pirate books to create a permanent central library. While blocking the piracy of work to train AI, Alsup justified the legal acquisition of books to train Claude’s Large Language Models (LLMs) as fair use. He compared AI training to how humans can read, internalize and remember a book’s themes and style. “Like any reader aspiring to be a writer, Anthropic’s LLMs trained upon works not to race ahead and replicate or supplant them — but to turn a hard corner and create something different,” he wrote. The $1.5 billion settlement went to authors and publishers of nearly 500,000 registered works. Wolff and 27 other authors say the settlement isn’t enough. “To put me to work that way, without remittance, is a form of slave labor,” said Wolff, professor emeritus of English and winner of the National Medal of Arts. “They’re using my work without paying for it. As time goes on, they’re going to make the lives of writers very difficult if there’s no fruit to their labor.”   10 of Wolff’s publications had been used for AI training without permission.  “[The settlement] still gives Anthropic pretty free rein to roam through our literature and basically take what they think will be useful and profitable for them,” Wolff said.  Wolff, along with English professor Chang-rae Lee, opted out of the Bartz settlement. In May 2026, they filed the separate non-class lawsuit Cruz v. Anthropic, seeking a jury trial for full statutory damages of up to $150,000 per infringed work, surpassing the approximate $3,000 of damages per work offered in the Bartz settlement. Similar to the claims in Bartz, the plaintiffs allege that Anthropic illegally downloaded, reproduced and distributed their copyrighted books from “shadow libraries” like LibGen and PiLiMi, and that Anthropic broke the law by downloading and storing the pirated files in a central library. “Our agents didn’t think the blanket lawsuit covered quite enough of the liability to us and are seeking redress in more particular ways,” Wolff said.  If Wolff and his fellow authors are successful, they would gain a permanent injunction against Claude model training using their works.  Paul Goldstein, a Stanford Law leading scholar in intellectual property and one of the plaintiffs represented in the class action, acknowledged the difficulty of addressing and preventing copyright issues for AI companies.  “The essential problem … is what economists call ‘transaction costs,’” Goldstein wrote in an email to The Daily. “Millions of individual copyrighted works may be copied in the course of any training incident, and it’s simply impracticable for the platform to obtain licenses from the copyright owner of every — or, indeed, any — single work.”  Outside of Bartz and Cruz, many authors, visual artists and news outlets, including The New York Times and Getty Images, have filed over 70 infringement lawsuits against AI companies. While Bartz established the current rule for pirating books, the legal future of mass scraping AI models used to train LLMs remains uncertain.   The Authors Guild is also pursuing other lawsuits, including one against OpenAI and Microsoft, as part of a “multi-pronged approach to ensure that the law is clear that AI companies must license the books they use,” according to The Authors Guild Chief Executive Officer Mary Rasenberger. “Licensing allows authors and publishers to be compensated and to require the use of filters that ensure their works do not appear in outputs unless separately licensed,” Rasenberger wrote in an email to The Daily. The Authors Guild is working with Congress to create national legislation that will require licensing. “The Guild is up for the challenge,” Rasenberger wrote. “This is something we have been doing for 114 years, and the moment we are in today, while challenging, also presents opportunities for us to firmly realize our mission.” For Wolff, this support is critical for the next generation of writers. “I’m lucky that I’m able to have a life as a writer where I enjoy the profits of my work,” Wolff said. “I worry much more about the young writers I’ve worked with at Stanford and elsewhere being able to do that in the face of these technological challenges, because they’re very hard to grasp and to combat.” Some authors are waging these difficult legal battles to achieve a sense of credit for their work, outside of the settlement payment. “Attribution … is very important to the vast majority of authors, and not just academic authors,” Goldstein wrote. “The great majority of countries have something called the ‘moral right of attribution’ on the books to ensure that authors are credited for their work. The U.S., alone among industrialized nations, has no such moral right, which is a terribly unfortunate situation for authors generally.” As Stanford authors and AI companies continue to navigate copyright challenges for training, both sides must navigate a “foreign land,” Wolff said, meeting at the intersection of creative rights and technological growth. April Yu ('30) is a Columnist for Arts & Life (vol. 270) and a contributor to the News section of The Daily. She is an intended Human Biology and English major from New Jersey. title: Amazon Is Gutting Its AI Division After Sustained Failure
body_text: Amazon Is Gutting Its AI Division After Sustained Failure IG BS FB AI Society Health Machines Science Space Transport Latest Newsletter Search for: AI Anthropic Ethics Facial recognition Google Machine Learning Meta OpenAI xAI Society Art Blockchain Cybersecurity Education FCC Finance Food Privacy The Industrialists Virtual Reality Health Brain Developments Genetics Medical Prosthetics and Devices Sleep Studies Machines Computing Robotics Science Agriculture Biology Chemistry Energy Environment Evolution Future Materials Military Physics Space Astronomy Astrophysics Blue Origin Boeing ESA NASA Off-World Space Force SpaceX Transport Electric Vehicles Mass Transit Self-Driving Vehicles Tesla Latest Newsletter Artificial Intelligence Machine Learning Hardly Knew Ye Amazon Is Gutting Its AI Division After Sustained Failure Wait, Amazon has AI models? By Joe Wilkins Published Jul 29, 2026 1:57 PM EDT Add Futurism (opens Google in a new window or tab) More information Adding us as a Preferred Source in Google by using this link indicates that you would like to see more of our content in Google News results. By now, you’d be hard pressed to find anyone who isn’t broadly familiar with the AI heavyweights and their flagship models. OpenAI has ChatGPT, Anthropic has Claude, Google has Gemini. But what does Amazon have? Not a whole lot, it turns out. Unlike its competitors in the tech megacorp scene, Amazon’s standout AI model — organized under the name “Nova” — is about the farthest thing from a household name. And that’s not likely to change anytime soon, because the ecommerce giant is now gutting its in-house AI labs, Bloomberg reports . Per the outlet, Amazon is scaling back the ambitions of most of its Nova AI models and reorganizing its AI development teams as part of an effort to narrow its focus on “highest priority” goals, after its power-hungry large language models turned out to be a bust. Accordingly, the company has put most of its AI models on ice, Amazon insiders told Bloomberg . This includes its text-based Nova models, as well as video- and image-generating models, all of which have been placed in a state of “keep the lights on,” meaning they’re technically still supported, but only receive the bare minimum resources needed to sustain them. Instead, labor and computing power are being diverted toward a singular “frontier-model effort” led by Pieter Abbeel, director of the Berkeley Robot Learning Lab whose robotics company Covariant was hoovered up by Amazon in 2024. At the time Abbeel joined the tech giant, Covariant’s founders were working on AI models for robots, which lines up pretty well with Amazon’s push to automate everything it possibly can. News of the shift in Amazon’s strategic focus comes a week after it closed one of its key AI offices in San Francisco, an 80-person site specializing in research on artificial general intelligence, the supposed next-level of AI development where the tech obtains human-level intelligence and reasoning skills. With urgent questions swirling over whether LLMs can ever usher in a return on investment — let alone AGI — it may be that Amazon is jumping out of the AI hype cycle while it still can. Content from Discoverable Servers Easier to Discover Kelsey Duncombe-Smith October 27, 2026 Discoverable Servers are the most public spaces on Discord, with at least 1,000 members. Their admins chose to list them in Server Discovery so anyone can join them, no invite link needed. Discussions in Discoverable Servers will soon be easier to find when you search the web, so you can find the answer you’re looking for and step straight into the conversation on Discord. Admins and members can decide if and how their content is shared, and those controls start rolling out today, ahead of any changes. TL;DR: Help people find your community with Server Web Pages. A Server Web Page is a page on the web that describes a Discoverable Server, so people can decide whether they want to join. Starting November 16, 2026, all Discoverable Servers will have a Server Web Page. These pages may also display summaries of discussions happening in public channels (those visible to everyone in the server), to give a better sense of what people are talking about. Some messages from public channels may show on Server Web Pages and in web search beginning in mid-December 2026. The rollout is gradual, so it may be a few weeks before the first messages start appearing on the web. Server admins can opt channels out starting today, before anything goes live on November 16, 2026. Controls for admins are in Server Settings > Web Presence. You can choose which channels take part, or opt all channels out. If you don’t change anything, public channels stay on, and your Server Web Page goes live on November 16, 2026, if you don't already have one. Users have control over whether their messages are shown. If you'd rather your messages weren't shown, you can turn that off starting today in User Settings > Data and Privacy , before messages start rolling out in mid-December 2026 (or anytime after). One setting covers Channel Messages in every Discoverable Server. Channel Summaries are generated separately, from broader channel topics, and will still appear on Server Web Pages unless admins choose to turn them off. Usernames and avatars won't be shown alongside messages on Server Web Pages Private servers, DMs, and GDMs are always private and not included in these changes. These changes are limited to Discoverable Servers. How servers work today Over the years, Discord has built different kinds of spaces, so every group can decide how big the party gets and who can find it: Most servers are small, private spaces. They're meant for you, your friends, and nobody else. Community Servers are for bigger groups , with the tools to handle a crowd. Though someone still has to send you an invite link. Discoverable Servers are the most public spaces on Discord . To qualify, a server needs at least 1,000 members, has to be at least eight weeks old, and must meet activity and safety requirements . Anyone can find and join them, no invite link needed. Today’s announced features only apply to this type of server. Today, there are more than 63,000 Discoverable Servers, spanning communities from speedrunning to language learning to niche corners of every fandom. People find their way into communities they'd never have stumbled across otherwise. Until now, that's all being Discoverable meant. Why this matters Server Discovery was built for finding servers, not answers. Ever wanted to look up tricks for a faster speedrun? Or whether a powerful item is worth grabbing, or if it will completely ruin your build? Someone has almost certainly already answered it in a channel somewhere, in one of 63,000 Discoverable Servers. It can just be hard to find. Prior to Discord's launch, message boards were common, ranging from community-driven forums to official ones run by game studios. These message boards excelled at hosting long-form, structured conversations about helping people, theory crafting, and more. While they still exist today, many have moved into Discord servers. This has led to valuable information being locked in Discord conversations, inaccessible to the wider internet. We want to fix this. By giving admins the option to make certain channels discoverable from the web, we can help more people find and benefit from the knowledge shared in Discord communities. We expect this to help different types of communities in various ways: For fandoms, you can make specific channels an easy-to-find resource that answers the top questions new players ask. For content creators, you can more easily promote events and new content drops. For indie game developers, you can use public channels, including forums, to share updates and wiki-style information about your games. What's new for Discoverable Servers? Server Web Pages live on the open web and give people a glimpse of what a Discord community is about before they join. They’ve been available to Discoverable Servers for some time, but setup takes a few steps, so not every Discoverable Server has created one. Learn more about Server Web Pages . Starting from November 16, 2026, every Discoverable Server will have a Server Web Page. If you’re an admin and have already set one up, you don't need to do anything. If you don’t have one and want to get a head start on how your community shows up to the rest of the internet, you can go through the setup process today and publish it in a few clicks. If your moderation team doesn't set one up beforehand, a default page goes live for you on November 16, 2026, using details from your Server Profile. You can edit it whenever you like. Having a Server Web Page is a core part of being a Discoverable Server. If you don't want one, you can always switch back to being a Community Server . Server Web Pages are also getting more useful. Until now, your Server Web Page has shown a small description of what your community is about. From November 16, 2026, it may also start showing what your community is talking about. Including this helps someone with a question find their way to your community if it already has the answer. Channel Summaries. These show a small slice of what's being talked about in your server, directly on your Server Web Page. These automated summaries focus on active conversations from November 16, 2026, onwards. Admins can change which channels they draw from, curate the summaries that are shown, or turn them off entirely. Usernames and avatars will not be shown in summaries. Channel Messages. From mid-December 2026, answers to questions your members sent in public channels can be found in a web search, in their own words. Server admins decide which channels take part, and server members can choose whether their own messages appear. Usernames and avatars will not be shown alongside these messages. You can already see an early version of this on a few Server Web Pages. We’ve been piloting Channel Messages with Discoverable game communities, including NBA 2K , Rust , and Dead by Daylight . (During this pilot, all posts were from admins and moderators, not members.) If you're running a community, useful answers to common community questions can show up in web search: how to unlock an easter egg, new builds or strategies, or a boss guide. Someone looking for help will be able to find a real answer from a real person, and can step straight into the conversation that it came from by clicking through and opening Discord. What does this mean for Discoverable Server members? Starting mid-December 2026, if a server’s admins allow it, messages from public channels can appear on Server Web Pages and in search results, without usernames and avatars. Messages you sent before then won’t be shown. Channels where content may appear on the web will be labeled, so you know before you send a message. If you'd rather your messages weren't shown, you can turn that off today in User Settings > Data and Privacy . One switch covers every Discoverable Server you're a part of. We're rolling this out gradually, so it may be a few weeks before the first messages from those channels go live. Learn more . What can admins do now? Your server controls start rolling out today , in Server Settings > Web Presence. You can choose which channels take part, or turn them all off. If you don’t change anything, public channels stay on, your Server Web Page goes live on November 16, 2026 (if it's not already published), and Channel Summaries can start the same day. Channel Messages start rolling out in mid-December 2026. You can adjust your Channel Summaries and Channel Messages settings before they roll out. And if you'd rather publish your Server Web Page yourself, you can do that today. See the full details in our Help Center . However you set things up, we hope this is a step toward bringing back what made forums great: answers anyone can find, and an open door to the community that wrote them. Frequently Asked Questions How will I know if I am in a server that allows content to appear on the web? Discoverable Server admins choose which channels to make available on the web.Those channels will be labeled, so you’ll know before you send a message. As always, you can customize your own privacy choices in your user settings under Data & Privacy. What if I decide later that I don’t want my messages shown on the web? You can turn off your Channel Messages setting anytime in User Settings > Data and Privacy . Messages you send after that won’t appear on the web. Messages you sent while it was on stay up unless you delete them from Discord. Messages from before mid-December 2026 aren’t included, regardless of your setting. Learn more . Does this work the same way in every region or for every user? ‍ In the EU, UK, Canada, Brazil, Australia, and South Korea, the member setting for Channel Messages is off by default given legal restrictions, so members’ messages won’t appear on the web unless they turn it on. Users in the teen age group are excluded completely and cannot enable Channel Messages until they’re an adult. Everywhere else, it’s on unless members turn it off. Other than that default, everything works the same way in every region. Learn more . Tags No items found. title: The Mythical Man-Month in the Age of AI
body_text: The Mythical Man-Month in the age of AI - Jan van den Berg Jan van den Berg Home About Quotes Search 🇳🇱 RSS The Mythical Man-Month in the age of AI 27 October 2026 Last weekend I watched four people desperately trying to get a laptop to connect to a screen. I was happily observing their efforts, with zero intent to join in. But someone nudged me: can't you have a look at it? My reply: "Haha sorry no! My experience is that adding more people will not solve this problem any quicker". I was of course -- indirectly -- referring to Brooks's Law: "Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later." It was formulated by computer scientist Frederick P. Brooks Jr. in his 1975 book The Mythical Man-Month, based on his experience managing the IBM OS/360 project. However I got to thinking. Does this still hold up in the age of AI agents and LLMs? At first glance, you’d think no. The traditional bottlenecks -- onboarding time, endless stand-ups, and office politics -- disappear overnight. An AI agent is up to speed in milliseconds and doesn't demand a coffee break. But when you look closer, and the law hasn't vanished. It just mutated. The famous "Baby Problem" remains: nine agents still can’t deliver a baby in one month. Sequential tasks are still sequential. Overhead hasn't disappeared; it shifted: instead of managing people, you are now managing agents. Someone still needs to define "done", review the code, catch hallucinations, and stitch the pieces together. That someone is you. Throw nine autonomous agents at a single codebase without crystal-clear orchestration, and they will happily rewrite each other's work in a high-speed loop. Maybe the 2026 update to Brooks’s Law should be: "Adding agents to a project with unclear requirements gets you the wrong answer faster." ⬅ Previous post Interview with Ondřej Surý in the Atlantic © 2026 Jan van den Berg

title: Police are using AI to pull over drivers for 'suspicious' behavior
Three new discoveries in mathematics, computer science, and physics
body_text: Working with academic communities to build scientific understanding | OpenAI Skip to main content Research Products Business Developers Company Foundation (opens in a new window) Log in Try ChatGPT (opens in a new window) Research Products Business Developers Company Foundation (opens in a new window) Try ChatGPT (opens in a new window) Login OpenAI October 26, 2026 Research Publication Working with academic communities to build scientific understanding Loading… Share Local smoothing and the Kakeya conjecture Local smoothing and the Kakeya conjecture The Exponential Time Hypothesis is false Existence of quantum chromodynamics and completions of the Standard Model Supporting scientists Local smoothing and the Kakeya conjecture The Exponential Time Hypothesis is false Existence of quantum chromodynamics and completions of the Standard Model Supporting scientists We are announcing three new discoveries in mathematics, computer science, and physics about harmonic analysis, complexity theory, and quantum field theory. Our release process continues to evolve in response to feedback from the associated academic communities. In our view, these manuscripts are best understood as a form of raw research data. To convert this raw research data into scientific understanding, in this release we are experimenting with a new approach. We reached out to external experts and asked them to act as shepherds, organizing groups to understand the new results. They advised three different release strategies: For the math result, release the AI output, leaving researchers free to organize their own efforts to explain the result. For the computer science result, form an external group of collaborators to explain the result, while making the AI output publicly available for anyone to examine and build on. For the physics result, form an external group of collaborators and defer to them on the release of materials. We do not yet know which of these three approaches will be most useful, and we welcome feedback on what works and what we can improve. The external collaborations will follow four principles: Transparency. We are transparent about the existence of our collaborations. Participants will not be asked to sign nondisclosure agreements and will be free to discuss the work, share intermediate products, and publish their conclusions. No Academic Credit. We do not seek academic credit for the discoveries produced by our internal models. Inviting a researcher to help steward a collaboration also does not imply that they or their working group made the original discovery. Recognition. This group should receive recognition for the understanding they develop, the writeups they author, and the other materials they create. The group will also help ensure that the work appropriately credits researchers, techniques, and ideas that it draws on. Independence. Participation is voluntary and unpaid. Working-group members participate independently, and their conclusions are their own. They do not speak on behalf of OpenAI, and OpenAI does not speak on their behalf. We will turn over materials and artifacts related to these results to the collaborations. For the computer science collaboration, the group has decided to make the natural language proof and Lean formalization public immediately, and we are publishing them directly to our GitHub repository. For the physics collaboration, the group has decided to hold off on releasing the AI-produced artifacts and instead work on writing it up themselves. All of these approaches involve tradeoffs. On the one hand, the collaborations empower experts to foster unpacking the results and contextualizing them in the broader academic community. On the other hand, choosing initial shepherds necessarily shapes who gets involved first and creates asymmetry of information. We welcome feedback on how to broaden participation and make this process more useful. Local smoothing and the Kakeya conjecture The result in mathematics concerns harmonic analysis. In 1991, Sogge proposed the local smoothing conjecture, which concerns the behavior of waves as they become focused. In particular, the conjecture states that the most extreme focusing must be short-lived. The amount of focusing at a typical random time is always much smaller than what can happen at the worst-case time. This is a familiar pattern throughout mathematics: what can happen in the worst case is more extreme than what is observed after averaging. Because of how fundamental this conjectured phenomenon is, it also has wide ranging implications throughout mathematical analysis. For instance, it implies the Kakeya conjecture and Stein’s restriction conjecture. In 2019, Guth, Wang, and Zhang ⁠ (opens in a new window) proved the local smoothing conjecture in two spatial dimensions. In 2025, Wang and Zahl ⁠ (opens in a new window) proved the Kakeya conjecture in three dimensions. Our models produced a proof of the local smoothing conjecture in every dimension and therefore also resolve the Kakeya conjecture and Stein’s restriction conjecture in all dimensions. The new proof is based on a novel auxiliary partial differential equation. We obtained our AI output on October 18th, 2026, which was formalized in Lean the following day, and then we reached out to an expert to discuss forming a collaboration around this result. Following their recommendation, we decided to release the AI output publicly, following the same strategy for this result as our October 6th, 2026 release ⁠ . We have released both an AI natural language output writeup ⁠ (opens in a new window) produced by our models and a Lean proof ⁠ (opens in a new window) in our public GitHub repository. The Exponential Time Hypothesis is false The computer science collaboration will understand and explain a result concerning the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), a longstanding conjecture about the computational complexity of Boolean formula satisfiability, a problem deeply related to the P vs. NP problem. The ETH has been widely believed to be true, and has been used in hundreds of papers to derive conditional computational hardness results across a wide variety of fields including graph theory, computational biology, databases, computational geometry, and more. Surprisingly, our system has recently proved that the ETH is false, a result that was subsequently verified in Lean. The refutation of the ETH reopens questions about how much faster these tasks could become, and may help guide the search for better algorithms. Finding such algorithms, and turning theoretical advances into practical improvements, will require significant further research. This work will be verified and shepherded by a group led by Russell Impagliazzo (UC San Diego), Ramamohan Paturi (UC San Diego), and Ryan Williams (MIT). All three are experts in algorithm design and complexity theory. Impagliazzo and Paturi, along with Francis Zane, are the original proposers of the Exponential Time Hypothesis, and have authored a number ⁠ (opens in a new window) of influential ⁠ (opens in a new window) ⁠ (opens in a new window) papers ⁠ (opens in a new window) on the topic ⁠ (opens in a new window) over the last 30 years. Williams has refuted strong ⁠ (opens in a new window) ⁠ (opens in a new window) versions ⁠ (opens in a new window) of the ETH, used ETH for hardness ⁠ (opens in a new window) ⁠ (opens in a new window) results ⁠ (opens in a new window) , and connected algorithms ⁠ (opens in a new window) and lower bounds ⁠ (opens in a new window) . We have agreed to the group’s requests that all raw data of the results be made public to facilitate independent verification by the community, and that OpenAI commit to funding a conference to understand the implications of this work on the field as a whole. The group invites the community to help organize an open examination of the ETH claim and to discuss the broader questions that AI-generated breakthroughs raise about verification, access, credit, and the future of research. Our AI found its natural language disproof for the ETH on October 16th, 2026 and then subsequently we formalized the result in Lean on October 17th, 2026, which led us to develop the collaboration described here. To that end, we have released both an AI natural language output writeup ⁠ (opens in a new window) produced by our models and a Lean proof ⁠ (opens in a new window) in our public GitHub repository. Computational complexity has many open questions and conjectures, whose proofs or refutations have so far eluded the best efforts of scientists. We hope that humans with AI can provide new understanding in this field, and shed light on the inherent capabilities and limits of efficient computation. Existence of quantum chromodynamics and completions of the Standard Model The physics collaboration will understand and explain a result that gives a mathematically rigorous existence proof of certain interacting quantum field theories containing gauge fields and fermions in four dimensions, including Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and a unified completion of the Standard Model of particle physics. Our work builds on Balaban’s approach ⁠ (opens in a new window) in constructive quantum field theory. As a subproblem, this work also includes a proof of the existence of pure Yang–Mills theory, which is part of the Quantum Yang–Mills Theory Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize problem ⁠ (opens in a new window) . The Standard Model describes the interaction of fundamental subatomic particles for three of the four fundamental forces, excepting gravity. The existence proof pertains to the simplest grand unified theory that includes the gauge fields and fermions of the Standard Model (as the Standard Model itself cannot be extrapolated to arbitrarily short distances). QCD describes the interaction of particles such as quarks and gluons via the strong force. Pure Yang–Mills theory only describes the self-interactions of the gluons, the force carriers, rather than matter such as quarks. David Gross will lead a group including Michael Douglas, Arthur Jaffe, Igor Klebanov, and Nikita Nekrasov that will shepherd this work. Gross’s 1973 work on asymptotic freedom in Yang-Mills theories helped establish QCD as the theory of the strong interactions and earned him a share of the 2004 Nobel Prize in Physics ⁠ (opens in a new window) . Asymptotic freedom is also the key mechanism underlying the existence of these theories as mathematically rigorous objects. Jaffe formulated the Quantum Yang-Mills Theory Millenium Prize problem ⁠ (opens in a new window) with Witten and also envisioned the idea of Millennium Prize problems and co-founded the Clay Mathematics Institute. Douglas has already been a steward of this problem over the last 20 years, reporting on its status in 2004 ⁠ (opens in a new window) and then providing a comprehensive update on the progress ⁠ (opens in a new window) at the beginning of this year. Klebanov helped pioneer the application of gauge–string duality to confinement, an important property of QCD, and now directs the Simons Collaboration on Confinement and QCD Strings ⁠ (opens in a new window) , Nekrasov has done groundbreaking work on exact methods for generalizations of Yang–Mills theory and won the Dannie Heineman Prize for Mathematical Physics in 2023. The group requests that all communications with any and all members of the group regarding this effort be directed to the following email account: YANGMILLS4D@gmail.com. Our models produced a natural language proof for Yang–Mills existence on September 9th, 2026, and then subsequently produced a proof for QCD on September 18th, 2026. Given the length and complexity of the work, we postponed release until the Lean formalization completed. We finished our formalization of Yang–Mills’ existence on October 16th, 2026, which led us to develop the collaboration described here. We hope that these results mark the beginning of a transition in which quantum field theory, the most important framework in modern theoretical physics, becomes a mathematically rigorous field. We are excited to provide resources for academic-led progress towards that goal. Supporting scientists We are committed to supporting the broader work of understanding and building on these results. These collaborations complement our recently announced $5 million contribution ⁠ (opens in a new window) to the Simons Foundation. Managed and awarded by the Simons Foundation, that funding will support workshops, conferences, and special programs to help researchers understand and build on results produced by AI. We are committed to ensuring funding for researchers to independently examine, explain, and build on the results above. We continue to invite feedback on the best way to disclose results and engage with scientists to accelerate discovery. 2026 Author OpenAI Keep reading View all Sharing AI progress in mathematics Research Oct 6, 2026 Advisory group on mathematics and artificial intelligence Company Sep 21, 2026 Using thousands of AI agents to uncover new leads in biological data Publication Oct 21, 2026 Research Research Index Research Overview Economic Research Latest Advancements GPT-6.1 Sol GPT-6 Astra GPT-5.6 GPT-5.5 Safety Safety Approach Deployment Safety (opens in a new window) Security & Privacy Trust & Transparency Products ChatGPT (opens in a new window) ChatGPT Business (opens in a new window) ChatGPT Enterprise (opens in a new window) ChatGPT for Education (opens in a new window) Codex Dots (opens in a new window) Release Notes API Platform Overview API Log In (opens in a new window) Docs (opens in a new window) Business Overview Solutions Resources Plugins Customer Stories Partner Network Contact Sales Developers Plugins (opens in a new window) Models (opens in a new window) Docs (opens in a new window) Resources (opens in a new window) Developer Forum (opens in a new window) Company About Us Our Charter Careers News Support Help Center (opens in a new window) OpenAI Status (opens in a new window) More Stories Academy Supply Co. title: Software may be getting worse, but it used to be horrible
body_text: Software may be getting worse, but it used to be horrible - bitlog.com Skip to main content bitlog.com Jake Voytko's personal log of bits Home About me Software may be getting worse, but it used to be horrible Written by Jake Voytko on October 27, 2026 Software is degrading all around us, for obvious reasons. I've written about this before. All else equal, if you increase your code production by 10x but you don't reduce your error rate by a factor of 10, then your production app is buggier than it used to be. I've seen threads where people also have some nostalgia for the past: "software used to be better in the past" or "we've forgotten how to program like we used to" or "software quality has been declining for decades." And as someone who has used computers since 1990, I'm here to disabuse you of this notion. Software was horrible. Everything crashed all the time. Yes, there were great programmers like John Carmack who could keep the entire program in their head and iterate on thoughtful codebases over decades. No, they did not write a majority of the software that we used to use. Historical context Almost everyone in the world was on Windows. Windows peaked around a 95% market share, plus or minus a few percentage points based on your source. Yes, you probably knew someone with an iMac who would tell you that it was way better than a Windows machine, and they could prove it if anyone ever actually released applications for Macs. And yes, there were Linux distros like Debian where people could get real computing done [0] . But those were exceptions. Almost every computer user had a Windows machine and either an Intel or an AMD processor. And Windows had a lot of problems. There was one saving grace though: companies only got one chance to ship their software. At a certain point, it was going to be loaded onto a floppy disk or burned onto a CD or a ROM, put into a box, and mailed out. And that version had to work out of the box. So there was some quality floor that you couldn't slip below. How bad did it get? Here's a collection of things that I remember. This isn't linear; it's my collection of memories from 1990 and onward. Blue Screen of Death Windows had extreme stability issues for most of my childhood. Let me introduce you to the song of my people, the Blue Screen of Death. The blue screen of death in Windows XP, Vista and 7, courtesy of Wikipedia This was Windows' version of a kernel panic. It happened right when you were in the middle of something. Or maybe you were doing nothing. It didn't matter: the blue screen was coming. Your computer crashed for a lot of reasons. First, device drivers. If you bought some new peripheral like a joystick, it'd come with a floppy disk or CD with device drivers. You'd dutifully install them. The device drivers had the same function as they do today: they help the operating system understand how to interface with the hardware. This might get you thinking, "Oh wow, so they sent out the device drivers on physical media? You can't update a physical disk once you ship it. Surely they took extra care to get everything right." My friend, this could not be further from the truth. I'm sure there were good drivers and bad drivers. But in aggregate, they were buggy, and it only took one marginal device driver to destabilize your computer. The Windows operating system also had its own code quality issues back then, and would sometimes fail to fully reclaim resources from programs that exited. So your computer would slowly degrade over time until eventually the slow rot would take down your machine. All in all, your computer would just blink out of existence from time to time. It was a fact of life. Autosave Do you know what pairs really well with a computer that crashes all the time? Applications that don't autosave. Even better, applications with autosave that don't flush buffered writes and corrupt their save files. It was commonplace to get into the zone and work on a document for hours, and then suddenly you would get either a Blue Screen of Death, or a pop-up saying that your application had a problem and had to exit. And you'd scream and you'd double-click your document over and over, but it was no use. You had to start over. But there was a consolation prize. It was your turn to tell everyone, "I was working on a document for THREE HOURS! And then the computer crashed and I lost everything. It was all gone. I had to redo it." There was always that one asshole that was like "why didn't you save?" But you didn't get mad. You knew that he was 2 weeks from having the same thing happen to him. When I joined the Google Docs team back in 2010, we instrumented the Ctrl+s keyboard shortcut for fun. It didn't do anything but record a metric saying that it had been pressed. This "save" keyboard shortcut was in the top 5 non-editing user actions, just behind things like "move the cursor with arrow keys." And it did absolutely nothing. Google Docs autosaves. But everyone was so traumatized from years or decades of losing work that they reflexively saved anytime they edited anything. Nothing was secure When my sister and I were little, we loved going into stores with display units. The computers would often have games installed you could play. Worst case, you could always open up MS Paint or Solitaire and mess around for a few minutes. One time, we were in a store where the display models had password-protected screensavers. My sister was undeterred. She just hit Ctrl+Alt+Del, selected the screensaver application, and clicked "End Task." And we were in. The best minds of Microsoft were nothing next to the hacking talent of a 9-year-old. And this is the level of security that your computer afforded you. If you used the Internet for long enough, your computer would start to collect a bunch of advertising malware. When you turned your computer on, you would start to see pop-ups and pop-unders with random ads, even when you weren't using browsers. So you'd do another antivirus scan, or later on you could visit websites that could also run the malware scans for you. And not to mention the viruses that would drop the Internet to its knees once a year by doing trivial things like "adding a macro to a Word document that sends emails." Disk fragmentation Any techie can remember going to a nontechnical relative's house. In some dusty corner, they'd have an ancient Windows computer barely hanging on by a thread. It would literally take 20 minutes to turn on. You'd sigh and say, "let me fix this for you." You would open two programs. This would take about 5 minutes. The first program emptied cache files and the Recycle Bin. The second was Disk Defragmenter. Your computer slowly became unusable if you never saw this window. Back in the day, hard drives in Wintel boxes stored data with spinning magnetic platters. The hard drive had a retractable arm with a little magnetic reader, and it would read data by retracting the arm to the right position and then moving the disk to the start of a sector. But of course, as you add more and more files, the game of Tetris doesn't work, and the rest of your file doesn't neatly fit onto the disk before the next file's record begins. So your file would end up in two (or more) places on the hard drive. This was called fragmentation. A little bit of fragmentation was unavoidable, but if more and more files became fragmented then your computer became slower and slower until eventually Grandpa's computer took 20 minutes to start. Many modern filesystems, Windows' included, automatically handle defragmentation in the background nowadays. But Windows did not back then. You needed to periodically manually start the defragmentation process yourself. By the time I got into college, I discovered that Windows had a scheduler and could run Disk Defragmenter whenever I wanted, so I just left my computer on all the time and let it defragment at 5 in the morning. Phenomenal cosmic power, itty bitty memory Applications were heavily memory constrained, so programmers tried to save bits and bytes everywhere. This should have been invisible to me, but it wasn't. At one point I had a crappy video game version of Axis and Allies for the PC, released in 1998 [1] . Imagine Risk but World War 2. And the AI was really bad, and could generally be beaten easily. But the game had a major flaw: If a country had more than 255 units, the whole game would crash. And naturally the AI also loved to turtle, so it was common for the AI to have a territory with over a hundred units that was impossible to wear down. So because of this programming choice, the game was a race to wipe out the enemy before it could force a stalemate by crashing the game. This kind of thing happened all the time. During my first programming class in my freshman year of high school, one of our lessons was effectively, "here's why you all recognize numbers like 128, 256, and maybe 65536." Software came on unreliable physical media Even if the software worked perfectly, you might scratch your game CD and lose the ability to play it. Then you'd start asking your friends if anyone had a spare copy of Red Alert or something, just so that you could finally finish the single-player campaign. This wasn't unique to CDs. Anything physical could degrade. My half-brother had a NES game called Dragon Warrior or something, but the cartridge was corrupted and there was no way to leave the first room. And even if you kept all of your games in good condition, the contacts inside of the NES that connected the cartridge to the console could rust and fail. This kind of thing happened all the time. "But Jake, that's hardware and not software." All I'm saying is that y our software was fragile and it needed to be protected and preserved. It's not like you had the option for a physical disk or the online install and you chose the disk. By the nature of distribution, the software itself would degrade and rot away from you. Online games assumed good behavior One of the earliest online games I played was Diablo II, which means that I have seen the true heart of darkness inside of humanity. Online games have a strange problem: gamers often don't want to be together. They just happen to cohabitate a space. And Diablo II had a lot of design features that lent themselves to chaos: There were rampant client-side hacks. In PVP servers, people would use hacks to e.g. fire tracking arrows far beyond the range that they should have been able to. All item drops were equally available to everyone in the server. That means when you got close to killing an act boss, you and your party would transition from allies to rivals and spam click when the boss finally popped. If you had a corpse on the ground and died again, you'd lose everything you had equipped. People would try to force you to have a full inventory by dropping a bunch of cheap items onto your corpse, hoping that you'd accidentally pick up common items before picking up your corpse. Then you'd try to pick up your corpse. You'd only pick up some of the items. Then they'd kill you a second time and you'd lose everything that you managed to pick up. The game had a lot of item duping glitches. As you can imagine, this ruined the in-game economy since it became dominated by the duped items. And it enabled a lot of scams. They'd pretend that they just duped an item, and they'd wait for someone to ask how they did it. Then they'd walk the user through step-by-step, but one step would involve dropping your item on the ground and then the scammer would pick up the item. There was no guild system, but people still ran guilds. This means that there was no trusted way to identify guaranteed friendlies. Many of these were fixed by the time Diablo III came around. They had extra guards against duplicated items. Bosses gave players individual drops, so there was no competition for items when you killed bosses. And you didn't need to recover items from your corpse in a way that risked you losing items. These were all hard-won lessons. Turbo button I started using my family's computer around 1990 when I learned how to read. The computer was a beige 286 that sat on our desk with the monitor perched on top. It had a 5.25" floppy drive. It had a power button. It had a reset button. And it had a TURBO button. The TURBO button was supposed to be ignored most of the time, but you could press it when you needed to slow the computer's processor down. Why would you need to do that? Because IBM's first desktop computers ran on the 8088 processor at 4.77MHz [2] . It didn't stay this way for long. But there was a problem: many programmers wrote their applications with the assumption that computers had that 4.77MHz processor. Programmers synchronized animations, video game frame rates, and generally relied on the assumption that they were working with a fixed clock speed. If you used one of these applications on a faster processor, they would likely be unusable. Computer manufacturers devised a simple solution: add a TURBO button that would just slow your CPU down on demand. Whenever you ran into an application that had timing issues, just press that TURBO button and watch it slow down to a comfortable speed. I never needed to actually press the TURBO button in anger. My understanding is that most of the applications that benefitted from the TURBO button were games, and we only played newer educational games that didn't have these timing issues. When editing this post, I thought about dropping this section a few times. But can you imagine having an "Original iPhone" button on the side of your iPhone so that the Notes app could work? Good grief. Modern software isn't perfect Modern software isn't perfect. It's bloated. It's slow. It was written by too many people. It's too complex. It has too many cooks in the kitchen. And now, we're losing our grasp on how it works under the hood as we delegate more and more to the agents. But I'd never go back to the way software used to be written. Give me process isolation and online updates. Give me higher-level programming languages that abstract common pitfalls from C and C++. Give me game designers that handle timing using the system clock. Give me Steam and Windows Update. You can keep your old release process that fell by the wayside. Footnotes [0] From what I remember from trying to install Debian in my high school years, the most popular app on Linux was anything that could edit XF86Config . [1] I'm having trouble corroborating this anecdote with information I can find online. The details might not be exactly right. But this is what happened, to the extent that the memory survived 25ish years. [2] Not GHz, MHz!
