title: Roblox downloaded 145GB models from us (including adult content) without asking
body_text: Open3DLab • Roblox downloaded 145 GB of models from our sites (including adult content) without asking ⯆ Network Sites Open3DLab SmutBase SFMLab Discord Mastodon BlueSky OPEN3DLAB ⯆ Menu Browse Tutorials FAQ News Members ⯆ Account Create Account Sign in Roblox downloaded 145 GB of models from our sites (including adult content) without asking By Salaryman on October 26, 2026 Last updated on October 26, 2026 On 15 and 16 October 2026, a crawler that said it belonged to Roblox walked through almost every project on Open3DLab, SFMLab and SmutBase, and proceeded to download complete copies of 1,027 files from 712 projects. 145.5 GB of our creators' work, downloaded for what we assume are AI training purposes. This post briefly describes what happened, what mitigations were taken, and what this signals for the community at large. A more detailed writeup outlining what we saw in our logs will be posted at a later time. What happened On Sunday the 18th of October, we noticed a crawler making a large number of requests to our sites and download infrastructure. The crawler sent the same user agent on every request, trellis2-data-sourcing/1.0 (3D foundation model research; [redacted]@roblox.com) . It came from a single Amazon Web Services (AWS) address. It had read the main page of 18,926 projects, which is practically our entire catalogue, in 26,429 requests over a span of 34 hours. After pulling the project pages, it downloaded complete copies of 1,027 files from 712 projects, 145.5 GB in all, before suspending operations during the weekend. The downloads include 364 files (54.8 GB) from 224 projects on SmutBase, which hosts adult content only. With the SFMLab projects marked adult, 345 of the 712 projects (62.6 GB) are adult content. The main limiting factor in the number of files downloaded was the crawler's reliance on the free download servers, which have caps on speed limit and number of concurrent downloads. The crawler did not respect our robots.txt, (which it did retrieve), ignored our Terms of Service, (which forbid scraping), and defied the creators' licenses: 423 of the 712 projects are licensed for non-commercial use only. Within the sample it retrieved, it took adult projects at the same rate as everything else. Some examples include models of Eve from Stellar Blade , Mei from Overwatch , and a Horse cock dildo . Our response We found it on 18 October and blocked further attempts the same morning. The scraper had suspended its activity by that point, and we did not notice any scraper that weekend. We emailed the address in its user agent on 18 October and asked Roblox for comment. We have not had a reply. The crawler resumed scraping activity on October 19th, with all requests getting blocked by our servers. The scraper did not reduce its download attempts when faced with our blocks, and the scrapes seemed to fit neatly within office hours, only briefly pausing for an hour around lunchtime, and ending activity around the end of the workday (CEST). On the 20th, their scraper made its final return at 8:00, slowly tapering requests from lunchtime onward, likely in an effort to test our rate limiting. The requests stopped around 15:00. We sent another email to Roblox for questions, to which they again did not reply. Speculation This section contains our speculation and assumptions based on public information, and the information we noticed in our logs. Roblox has been building a "3D foundation model" since at least 2025.In March 2025 Roblox introduced Cube , which it calls its core generative AI system for 3D and 4D. The accompanying paper describes the goal as a foundation model for 3D intelligence. It lists character rigging among the things that model should eventually do, and generating characters and avatars as future work. Its first shape model was trained on roughly 1.5 million 3D assets from licensed and public datasets such as Objaverse, plus free assets from Roblox's own Creator Store whose creators had opted in. In February 2026 Roblox began rolling out "4D generation" built on Cube. The address in the user agent belongs to a researcher who is among the 40-plus authors of that Cube paper. The researcher's public professional profile says they are building a 3D foundation model at Roblox, and their earlier published work is on 3D reconstruction and real-time 3D rendering. We want to be clear: we don't suggest this researcher did anything on their own initiative or out of the ordinary for their job. A data-collection run like this is a company's decision, and the responsibility for it is Roblox's. But the profile says what the user agent says: the people behind this crawler build 3D foundation models. The "trellis2" in trellis2-data-sourcing may refer to TRELLIS.2 , an open 3D generation model Microsoft released in late 2025. It may mean the data was meant for training or tuning a model like it, or it may just be a project codename. We don't know. What we can say is that TRELLIS.2's published data toolkit contains no web crawler and no user agent, so this crawler and its label were written for the job. It is also possible that Roblox is re-using the Trellis.2 tooling for its own foundational model and it is re-using these scripts for its next model; the tools are open source. Our sites are full of things a 3D model-generation system needs and public datasets have relatively little of: complete, textured characters, many of them rigged, in the formats artists actually work in, each with a title, a description and preview images. Put together, we think the most likely explanation is that the crawler was collecting training or evaluation data for Roblox's 3D foundation model work. We can't prove it, and we don't know whether any of our creators' files ended up in a model. Roblox's track record This isn't the first time Roblox has been criticised for how it treats the people whose work its platform runs on, or for how it handles other people's rights. Young developers. In 2021 the games outlet People Make Games published a video investigation arguing that Roblox turns its young users into underpaid developers. By its calculation Roblox kept around 75% of the money spent in developers' games, against Steam's 30%, and paid creators in Robux, which they can only cash out once they've earned a minimum amount. Roblox declined to discuss its revenue share and payout minimums. (In September 2025 it raised its cash-out rate by 8.5%.) Copyright. In 2021 the US National Music Publishers' Association sued Roblox for at least $200 million over unlicensed music on the platform. The case settled later that year for an undisclosed amount. Child safety. In October 2024 the short seller Hindenburg Research accused Roblox of inflating its user numbers and of failing to protect children. Roblox called the report misleading and pointed out that its authors stood to profit from a falling share price. Since then the attorneys general of Louisiana , Kentucky, Texas and Florida, among other states , have sued Roblox over child safety, and private lawsuits have been consolidated in US federal court. These are allegations, not findings. None of this proves anything about the crawler, but it strengthens our opinion that Roblox is a deeply unethical business. It shows a company that has repeatedly been accused of putting growth ahead of the people its platform depends on. You see how this looks, right? More than a third of Roblox's daily users were under 13 in 2025, by its own figures. Its rules ban sexual content, and in 2025 it tightened them further . Roblox's crawler took 224 projects from a site called SmutBase, which describes itself as exclusively for adult content, and 121 more that are marked adult on SFMLab. It took them at the same rate as everything else: 345 of the 712 projects it downloaded from are adult content. The further scraping attempts did not discriminate between adult content either. We want to be careful here. We don't think Roblox set out to collect adult content, and we have no evidence that any of it reached a model or a product. The scrapes were likely automated. But that is exactly the problem: as far as our logs show, nobody checked. A crawler working for a company whose platform tens of millions of children use was pointed at an adult site, and it took explicit models without telling them apart from anything else. Models reproduce what they learn from. If adult training data reaches a model that generates assets for Roblox, the only thing between that data and children is whatever filter Roblox builds afterwards, because its data collection didn't filter anything. Furthermore, when a creator deletes a project, or we remove one for breaking our rules or after a copyright notice, it's gone from our sites, but remains in these datasets. One project the crawler took has already been disabled on SFMLab since. If Roblox still has its copy, that copy is still there. We're not against adult content. It's our bread and butter. We think consenting adults should be able to access and enjoy this content freely, without the government looking over their shoulder. What we object to is our adult sites being emptied into an exploitative gaming company's training data without anyone asking, and being mixed into content offered to literal children. For a company being sued by several US states over child safety, "our AI team bulk-downloaded an adult site without looking" is not a good position to be in. If the penalty for a crime is a fine, then that law only exists for the lower class. This section is opinion. Roblox isn't the worst offender in AI's appetite for other people's work, just the latest to turn up in our logs. It isn't the only AI company in them, either. In the month before we found trellis2-data-sourcing , Meta's AI crawler, Meta-ExternalAgent, made about 380,000 requests to our sites, almost all from Meta's own network, and loaded 211,000 project pages. We have since blocked their crawler as well. The Roblox trellis2 crawler is the first individual crawler we spotted that actually pulled assets uploaded by our users, in flagrant defiance of any copyright or license that might apply to it. It fits a broader context, of AI labs taking content without permission. Here's what the largest companies have been accused of, and in some cases have admitted: Meta downloaded at least 81.7 TB of pirated books by torrent from shadow libraries, including through Anna's Archive, according to court filings by the authors suing it. In June 2025 a judge ruled that training on the books was fair use on that record , while stressing that the ruling didn't make Meta's conduct lawful in general. Meta, again: the adult studio Strike 3 Holdings alleges that Meta torrented thousands of its films to train AI video models. Meta says the downloads were for individuals' "personal use". In June 2026 the court refused to dismiss the case . The irony is hard to miss: Strike 3 is best known for suing thousands of individual BitTorrent users. Nvidia contacted Anna's Archive about high-speed access to its collection of pirated books for training data, and management signed off soon after, according to an amended class-action complaint filed in January 2026. Nvidia argued that contacting a pirate site isn't infringement. The court has since largely refused to dismiss the case . Anthropic downloaded hundreds of thousands of pirated books. A judge found that training on books it had bought was fair use, but keeping a library of pirated copies was not. In July 2026 the court approved a $1.5 billion settlement , about $3,000 per book. Now compare how copyright treats everyone else. In the early 2000s Jammie Thomas-Rasset was ordered to pay $222,000 for sharing 24 songs. Internet activist Aaron Swartz faced federal charges carrying decades in prison for downloading academic articles. The Internet Archive, a nonprofit library, lost in court for lending scanned copies of books it owned. Meanwhile, the Internet Archive's online library gets repeatedly scanned by AI companies in return. We'll be honest about where we stand. We don't like copyright as it exists. We'd like to see it radically reformed, and we wouldn't mourn it if it were abolished. Our community lives in its grey areas every day: many of the models on our sites are fan ports of characters from commercial games, made out of love and shared for free. When a studio sends us a takedown notice, we comply. While we as small artists and fan communities get copyright used against us, the world's largest companies are committing copyright infringement at a scale unseen in human history. This has been the case since the invention of the internet of course; digital media make duplication, remixing and resharing trivial, but copyright law never caught up. Filesharing stabbed copyright in the gut. AI is just twisting the knife, and completes the creation an unequal system where copyright infringement is only a crime if you're a low net worth individual. So we aren't asking for stricter copyright laws, or stronger protection for copyright holders. That will only benefit the major entertainment companies like Disney and Adobe who have already stacked the deck in their favor, and are happily making deals with Big-Tech and crushing small creators in the process. We're pointing out that the copyright we have isn't applied equally, and is in practice a two tier system. Individuals face ruinous damages for minor infractions. The largest companies in the world face a cost to be negotiated after the fact, if anyone can afford to sue them. A law that only works downwards gives nobody a reason to respect it, and it can't last in this form. For time being, we'd like to ask Roblox to respect the norms of this community. You credit people. You respect the license they chose. If you want to use someone's work for something they didn't offer it for, you ask. Those norms cost nothing to follow, and Roblox's crawler followed none of them. This scrape attempt saturated the connections for our free download servers for a couple of days, causing problems for our community of legitimate human users. It shows a lack of respect for the people who make this site what it is. those who produced, shared and host the work that you were about to throw in your AI mixer. Questions for Roblox We're sad that the emails we sent to Roblox were not met with a timely response, and would thus like to publicly ask Roblox for its response. These are the questions we'd like Roblox to answer: Did Roblox run the trellis2-data-sourcing crawler? What was the data for? Has any of it been used to train or evaluate a model, and if so, which? Why did the crawler ignore our robots.txt rules and our Terms of Service? Did anyone review which sites the crawler would visit? Was adult content excluded at any stage? Will Roblox delete the files and anything derived from them, and confirm that in writing? Will Roblox respect our creators' license choices, NonCommercial in particular, from now on? We hope Roblox reaches out to us. Also, if you are a person with information on what Roblox is doing, or a fellow site owner who has been targeted, feel free to get in touch as well. We're eager to hear if there's more of a pattern to the scraper's behavior. We've kept the full export of the relevant log files for auditing by external parties if the need arises. About us Open3DLab, SFMLab and SmutBase are three community sites for free 3D resources, run by a small team. SFMLab started in 2014 for Source Filmmaker models. SmutBase followed in 2016 and is exclusively for adult content. Open3DLab, for general-purpose 3D work, joined in 2020. Creators upload characters, props, maps and environments, choose a license for each project, and anyone can download the files for free. All three sites are intended for adults only. About the redaction. The email address in the user agent is a Roblox employee's work address. We've removed the name: this article is about what the Roblox crawler did, not about one person. About Attribution. We take the user agent at face value. Anyone can type any email address into a user agent, and the crawler ran from Amazon's cloud, not from Roblox's own network. Nothing we've seen suggests impersonation, and the label fits Roblox's published research closely. Still, it is a self-description, and it's the first thing we'd like Roblox to confirm. title: A 28-Year-Old DOGE Operative Gutted USAID. HR Had No Record of Him Working There
body_text: A 28-Year-Old DOGE Operative Gutted USAID. HR Had No Record of Him Working There | WIRED Skip to main content THE WIRED APP IS HERE DOWNLOAD NOW » Menu WIRED SECURITY POLITICS THE BIG STORY BUSINESS SCIENCE CULTURE REVIEWS Menu WIRED Account Account Newsletters Security Politics The Big Story Business Science Culture Reviews Chevron More Expand The Big Interview Magazine Events WIRED Insider WIRED Consulting Newsletters Podcasts Video Livestreams WIRED Store Search Search Molly Knight Raskin Politics Oct 27, 2026 12:24 PM A 28-Year-Old DOGE Operative Gutted USAID. HR Had No Record of Him Working There Despite the agency's human resources department saying he hadn’t even been onboarded, Jeremy Lewin oversaw the destruction of USAID. It’s not clear he had the legal authority to do so. Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/Getty Images Comment Loader Save Story Save this story Comment Loader Save Story Save this story On March 18, 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio handed the reins of the US Agency for International Development to Jeremy Lewin, a 28-year-old graduate of Harvard Law School, former investment banker, and affiliate of Elon Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency . At the time, Lewin’s appointment drew criticism because of his lack of experience in government, diplomacy, or foreign assistance. But for career staff inside the agency, the issues surrounding Lewin’s new role were much more alarming than his thin résumé. For at least two months, USAID senior staff had no knowledge of how Lewin, who appeared at the agency one day as a policymaker on an obscure detail from the General Services Administration, could have suddenly begun wielding the powers of the agency’s top official. Internal USAID emails reviewed by WIRED reveal that during the three-week period of March 18 to April 4, during which Lewin began canceling lifesaving aid programs and personally signed off on the termination of thousands of USAID employees, he did not sign the paperwork typically required by law to begin work at the agency, despite repeated requests. In fact, his appointment was so mysterious that USAID security was unable to issue him an ID card because they had no records of his employment. Lewin, currently director of policy planning at the State Department, tells WIRED that prior to Rubio delegating powers to him, he was “both detailed and dual appointed to work at USAID by Secretary Rubio according to well-established authorities and with the advice of State Department and White House counsel.” Experts, though, say that while Lewin performed the duties of a top USAID leader under the title Rubio handed to him—deputy administrator of policy and programming and chief operating officer—it isn’t clear that he had the legal authority to do so. Questions about how DOGE affiliates like Lewin stepped into top roles at many federal agencies, including USAID, remain key to dozens of active lawsuits targeting DOGE and the Trump administration over federal workforce reductions, firings, and agency dismantlings. Lewin has said, in a declaration submitted to the court in J. Doe 4 v. U.S. DOGE Service , that he began serving at USAID as a senior adviser as well as a director for strategy and programs on January 28, 2025. On March 18, according to court filings, Rubio, in his role as USAID’s acting administrator, delegated the authority of the deputy administrator of policy and programming and chief operating officer to Lewin, and also signed a document appointing Lewin an “officer of the United States.” According to the emails reviewed by WIRED, on March 20, two days after Rubio placed Lewin atop the USAID hierarchy, White House liaison to USAID Adam Korzeniewski notified HR to begin the process of onboarding Lewin as a senior adviser performing duties as deputy administrator. Four days later, the emails reveal, after prompting from HR, Korzeniewski provided a proposed start date—March 18—and the next day, Lewin was sent a temporary job offer. By March 26, the emails show, Lewin still hadn’t accepted the job offer, and had not filed his OF-306 , the federal government's standard pre-employment background screening form; without this document, a federal agency cannot lawfully issue a final job offer or consummate an appointment. An HR executive noted in an email dated March 31 that Lewin had not completed the onboarding tasks required to initiate “the security reciprocity process,” which recognizes the transfer of an employees’ security clearance from one agency to another. (A detailing agreement between the GSA and USAID dated February 14—two weeks after Lewin says he began at USAID—specifes that “commencement of the detail is contingent upon the Detailee’s successful adjudication and receipt of any necessary security clearances and other pre-employment screening required by USAID.”) On March 28, Lewin signed a letter terminating all remaining USAID staff. And as he executed sweeping powers to liquidate all 60 of USAID’s overseas missions and cancel thousands of lifesaving projects worldwide, HR repeatedly followed up with Korzeniewski. More than a week after Lewin’s appointment, the emails show, a USAID official told Korzeniewski that the agency’s office of security was “unable to issue a USAID ID card to Jeremy Lewin as SEC [the agency’s secure database] did not have a record of Jeremy as an employee.” “Until you’re onboarded at USAID, you aren’t even in the system,” says Natalia Machuca, a 15-year agency veteran who hired many staff. “You can’t get a badge, get into your computer, or even walk around the building.” Lewin tells WIRED, “I was a regular government employee with a valid security clearance held by the State Department during this entire period. USAID HR was confused about this paperwork for a period of days, but this issue was cleared up once they were made aware of the dual appointment and my State Department position.” But according to a top executive in HR, no one from their office saw any delegation documents until late April 2025. As one longtime HR executive at the agency, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said of Lewin: “He was the equivalent of an administrative ghost.” “I think this creates a huge accountability problem if you have these actors who are making really consequential life-or-death decisions who didn't go through any standard confirmation process,” says Don Moynihan, a public policy professor at the University of Michigan, “or in this case didn't even complete their paperwork to become a formal employee.” Lewin—who a White House official says submitted all the paperwork required for employment and clearance—provided WIRED with two documents, both dated March 18, 2025. One is an appointment and compensation waiver, signed by Rubio, naming Lewin director of strategy and planning, and stating that he would not be paid “pursuant to, among other provisions of law, 22 U.S.C. § 2385(b).” The other is a standard appointment affidavit naming Lewin USAID’s director of strategy and programs. A signature on the form appears to be Rubio’s, with the title given as “HRO”—usually an abbreviation for human resources officer. The State Department did not answer questions about this document. To one former senior USAID official, Rubio’s use of 22 U.S.C. § 2385(b)—an obscure provision traditionally reserved for rapidly deploying emergency-response staff to disaster zones abroad—to appoint Lewin looks like a legal contortion. “It is so unconventional that I’d never seen it used before I got to USAID,” the official said. “It was created for the purposes of scaling up really quickly if there was some outbreak of a virus somewhere and they needed to bring people on, then let them go.” Brian Feinstein, a law professor at the Wharton School of Business, acknowledged that while using 22 U.S.C. § 2385(b) to appoint Lewin is complex, it appears to him to be legal. “Because Lewin's appointment is consistent with this law regarding USAID personnel,” he says, “his unusual status should not be a factor.” Outside of this point, legal questions also remain about Lewin’s actions at the agency before he was appointed by Rubio, and his failure to complete the onboarding required to begin his initial detail period at USAID. During this time he was part of a team that issued sweeping orders, including one to then acting administrator Jason Gray to lock all USAID staff worldwide out of email and all communication systems, which could have put many staff’s lives at risk, and to terminate 57 of the agency’s top officials. David A. Super, professor of law and economics at Georgetown University, describes Lewin’s failure to complete his onboarding as much more than an administrative slip-up. “You can’t just walk in the door of a federal agency and become an employee,” he says. Under federal law , a cabinet secretary can only assign the authority of a Senate-confirmed position such as USAID administrator to a subordinate official—an agency employee or officer who works under the supervision of a higher-ranking officer. These regulations, Super says, are a way for Congress to guarantee that “someone walking off the street should not be given these enormous powers.” Nina Mendelson, who teaches law at the University of Michigan, agrees. She says the administration appeared to be trying to bypass the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, a federal statute that dictates how temporary vacancies in Senate-confirmed executive branch positions are filled. “The FVRA specifies who may fill in, for a limited time, when a Senate-confirmed post is vacant,” she says. “The possibilities are a first assistant, someone holding another Senate-confirmed post, or a longtime civil servant in the particular agency. Lewin doesn’t seem to have been any one of those.” Lewin being placed atop USAID came in a specific context. In February 2025, shortly after the arrival of Lewin and other DOGE affiliates at the agency, two dozen current and former USAID employees and contractors sued Musk and DOGE in Maryland District Court. They successfully secured a preliminary injunction on March 18, on the grounds that special government employees —temporary hires from outside USAID and the government—lacked the authority to execute sweeping federal actions. That same day, Rubio delegated powers of the agency’s top job to Lewin. On March 28, the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals granted the Justice Department an emergency stay, pausing the injunction based on the administration’s argument that the actions were taken by Lewin in his role as a federally appointed official. In his declaration , Lewin wrote: “I am not, and have never been, an employee of Elon Musk or USDS,” adding, “I report directly and only to Acting Administrator Rubio” in his role at USAID. The ruling gave Lewin the green light to fire thousands of career civil service and Foreign Service staff that very day, but the legal battle didn’t end there. The district judge has since allowed thousands of affected employees to sue DOGE and the administration as a group and ordered the government to hand over a trove of internal documents. Kevin Byrnes, a veteran federal employment law attorney representing more than 170 former and current career USAID staff in a separate suit challenging DOGE’s role in the mass firings, says the fact that Lewin had not completed mandatory onboarding paperwork raises even more questions about the authority of nonconfirmed agency leadership, and potentially exposes Lewin personally. “If Lewin didn’t even fill out the papers and was not authorized to take these actions, then he could be exposed to personal liability,” says Byrnes, who is asking the court to reinstate all the plaintiffs to their USAID jobs, with back pay. By default, we will not use your inputs or outputs from our commercial products (e.g. Claude for Work, Anthropic API, Claude Gov, etc.) to train our models. Feedback When you provide us feedback via our thumbs up / down button, we will store the entire related conversation, including any content, custom styles, conversation preferences, or model settings, in our secured back-end for up to 5 years. title: A Man from the Future: Why Johnny Can't Stop Abstracting
Sebastian Raschka's from-scratch video course on building reasoning models
body_text: Build Your Own Reasoning Model: A Full Video Course Subscribe Sign in Building Reasoning Models from the Ground Up: A Full Video Course Eight videos and over 11 hours of coding, covering evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation in Python and PyTorch. Sebastian Raschka, PhD Oct 24, 2026 337 13 35 Share I have written a lot about reasoning models here over the last two years on Ahead of AI, including a recent article on mechanisms to control reasoning effort levels in contemporary LLMs . Reasoning models are still as relevant as ever. In fact, almost all current-generation LLMs today are reasoning models or offer a reasoning mode. For those who are interested in how reasoning models work, including inference scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation, I wrote my recent Build Reasoning Model (From Scratch), which implements these from the ground up in PyTorch, which, in my experience, is still the best way to understand and learn how things really work. Now, in the last few months, I also sat down and recorded accompanying lectures I wanted to share with you. So, below, you will find eight reasoning model-from-scratch coding videos (11 hours of content). We start with a pre-trained LLM and implement methods to evaluate and improve it in Python and PyTorch. So, if you enjoyed my Coding LLMs from the Ground Up course last year, this is essentially the sequel (but you can also watch it without the prior course as a prerequisite). I’m currently taking a short break and will be back soon with more exciting LLM research roundups next month. In the meantime, I hope you enjoy coding along! How LLMs, reasoning models, and agents relate and fit together As a small side note, and since I often get asked how reasoning models relate to today’s AI agents, here’s a short section on this before getting started with the videos. A reasoning model is essentially an upgrade from a conventional LLM, that is, adding more post-training via reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (and optionally inference scaling techniques) to make it more capable of solving more challenging problems. Classically, reasoning models are developed for math and code, but the capabilities can generalize to other problem domains as well. A reasoning model then functions as the engine inside an agent harness, where the agent harness is a software or tooling framework around the LLM/reasoning model to tackle even more challenging problems (bigger coding tasks, travel booking, and all other sorts of personal assistant tasks). The task of the harness is sophisticated context management and giving the LLM access to tools. Figure 1: An engine analogy for conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses. Figure from my Components of a Coding Agent article. In this analogy depicted in the figure above, the model is the engine, and the agent harness adds the machinery that lets us use it for various things (as an upgrade from a simple chatbot interface). An agent can use either a conventional LLM or a reasoning model, but reasoning models are the more typical choice as they are more capable. (As mentioned above, most current-gen LLMs are reasoning models with variable reasoning effort settings.) So, the bottom line is that reasoning models, as the “engine,” remain an important part of understanding modern LLM agents. The resources accompanying these topics shown above are: The Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) book and videos The Build A Reasoning Model (From Scratch) book (and videos below) The Components of a Coding Agent article on Substack The videos below focus on developing the reasoning model that can power such a system. Scope and prerequisites The reasoning-from-scratch videos focus on a small pre-trained Qwen3 model, where we implement the reasoning methods ourselves in Python and PyTorch. Starting with a pre-trained model lets us focus on the interesting part: evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation. Regarding the prerequisites, I recommend being comfortable with Python and PyTorch. I designed the reasoning materials as standalone content, so the previous Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch) content is recommended but not strictly required. Compute-resource-wise, you can work through the early text-generation and evaluation examples on a CPU. For the later experiments, especially training, a GPU makes the work much more practical. The first video covers the setup and some more recommendations; the repository also includes hardware and environment recommendations . Figure 2: An overview of the topics being covered. The companion book These videos accompany my book, Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) . If you like to read through the explanation in more detail and at your own pace, work through exercises, and so on, I recommend the book as a companion here. For the most in-depth learning experience, my suggestion is to read a chapter, work through its code alongside the corresponding video, and then try the exercises. The book is available from Manning and Amazon , and the print edition is in color! Figure 3: A random excerpt from the Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) print book. Thank you to everyone who has picked up a copy or recommended it to a friend. Your support helps me keep creating these materials. The videos As a last, quick side note before getting to the main videos below: For a shorter, more conceptual overview, I also recommend my AI Reasoning Models course on LinkedIn Learning (it should be free for 24h when accessing it via the link there, which shouldn’t then require a LinkedIn Premium subscription). The course is about 90 minutes and explains how reasoning models work, covering the main ideas behind inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation. It’s a good optional preview if you’d like the main ideas without working through the full implementations below. To get to the main part of this article, here are the eight main lecture videos. 1. Motivation and code setup The first video starts with an explanation of the relationship between conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agents. Next, the main topic of the video is setting up the coding environment. This includes installing the Python and PyTorch dependencies (with uv), among others. I also discuss hardware choices and common setup issues. Topics covered The relationship between conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses On the benefits of learning through code implementations The scope of this video series Installing Python dependencies Choosing hardware and checking CUDA or Apple Silicon support Using a remote GPU with VS Code and troubleshooting the environment Watch video 1 · Setup instructions 2. Loading a base model, text generation, and KV caching Before adding reasoning methods in the upcoming videos, we need a working base model. Instead of training it from scratch, since that would be a whole other book (see Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch) ), we start with a pre-trained model. Here, we load the pre-trained weights of a Qwen3 0.6B model. Then, we implement the text-generation process via a streaming text generator and add KV caching and model compilation to make text generation more efficient. These implementations give us the baseline and base components we will evaluate and improve in the following videos. Topics covered Encoding text as tokens and decoding it back into text Downloading Qwen3 weights and loading the model on the selected compute device Going over tensor shapes, logits, and next-token predictions Implementing greedy decoding and streaming text generation Handling end-of-sequence tokens and measuring generation speed Adding a KV cache to reuse attention keys and values Combining KV caching with torch.compile and comparing hardware performance Watch video 2 · Chapter 2 code 3. Building a verifier for evaluation and reinforcement learning In this lecture, we build a math-answer verifier step by step, from answer extraction to normalization and checking mathematical equivalence. We then use it to evaluate the model on MATH-500. We use this verifier to evaluate the base model’s performance on the MATH-500 evaluation dataset. However, the verifier also has a second job later in the series: providing the reward signal for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Topics covered Intro to verifiers and how they fit into LLM evaluation methods (other methods are covered in the book’s appendix) Reusing answer verification as a reward signal for RLVR (more on that in chapter 6) The verifier flow, including extracting final answers, normalizing answers and checking mathematical equivalence Building an answer grader and an evaluation loop for MATH-500 Comparing base and reasoning models on MATH-500 Watch video 3 · Chapter 3 code 4. Inference-time scaling: sampling and self-consistency Now we explore ways to improve answers while keeping the model weights fixed. But before implementing specific inference-scaling techniques, we first implement methods to generate diverse answers from the same prompt (this is standard practice in proprietary LLM chatbots, such as ChatGPT). Concretely, we implement temperature scaling, multinomial sampling, and top-p filtering to generate diverse responses. Then we combine multiple responses through self-consistency, using majority voting over their final answers. We also examine the tradeoff between answer accuracy and the extra computation needed to generate more candidates. Topics covered Comparing how additional compute benefits model performance during training and during inference A gentle intro to inference-scaling through chain-of-thought prompts Implementing temperature scaling and multinomial sampling to generate diverse answers Adding top-p filtering to control the quality of the diverse answers Combining candidate answers through self-consistency, one of the most popular inference scaling techniques Evaluating MATH-500 accuracy against the cost of additional inference compute Watch video 4 · Chapter 4 code 5. Inference-time scaling: scoring and self-refinement Building on the previous video, we implement scoring functions to compare multiple answers generated from the same prompt. We can also use these scoring methods to break ties in self-consistency (covered in the previous lecture). The scoring methods covered here include computing token and sequence log probabilities (this will also be relevant in the later reinforcement learning chapters). We then implement a self-refinement loop in which the model critiques an answer and attempts a revision. The evaluation lets us check how useful those additional steps are for our model. Topics covered Using scoring functions for comparing multiple answers and breaking ties Implementing a simple heuristic scorer Computing token probabilities and sequence likelihoods (also relevant for the following lectures) Using log probabilities for improved numerical stability Building a self-refinement loop for generating critiques and revised answers Evaluating self-refinement on MATH-500 Watch video 5 · Chapter 5 code 6. Reinforcement learning: implementing GRPO for RLVR In this lecture, we move on to implementing a training technique called Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). We first implement a simplified version of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), generate groups of responses, score them with our verifier, and use their relative rewards for the model weight updates during training. Topics covered Generating reasoning traces and understanding the relationship between answer lengths and problem-solving abilities Discussion and comparison of two important LLM post-training methods: Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) Turning verifier scores into rewards and relative advantages Computing sequence log probabilities and a simplified GRPO loss Assembling the training loop with logging and checkpoint saves Evaluating checkpoints and checking training stability and memory needs Watch video 6 · Chapter 6 code 7. Reinforcement learning: tracking, clipped policy ratios, and KL terms Now that we implemented the training loop in the previous lecture, we can revisit it and analyze the training runs in more detail. Concretely, this video adds more training metrics for inspection and analysis, including entropy and advantage statistics, clipped policy ratios, KL loss term values, and formatted rewards. We then review the training logs and evaluation results to understand what these additions do and whether additions such as clipped policy ratios and KL loss terms are helpful. Topics covered Running longer training experiments and interpreting their logs Tracking advantages and entropy to understand training behavior Implementing clipping in the policy loss and analyzing its effects Adding a KL loss term and discussing reward hacking Understanding limitations of the simplified KL formulation Implementing format rewards and conditioning them on answer correctness Comparing checkpoints on MATH-500 and exploring further GRPO research Watch video 7 · Chapter 7 code 8. Distilling a reasoning model Finally, we explore another way to train a small reasoning model, that is, learning from answers generated by a stronger (and bigger) teacher model. We discuss different forms of distillation, prepare reasoning data, and implement the supervised training loop. We finish this lecture and course by evaluating the distilled model on MATH-500 and comparing the results. This rounds out the series with an alternative to developing reasoning capabilities through reinforcement learning. Topics covered Comparing the different combination and approaches to distillation, including soft and hard distillation, and on-policy and off-policy distillation Creating and collecting teacher-generated answers for the MATH dataset (using DeepSeek R1) Preparing the distillation dataset, including tokenization and training/validation/test splits Computing answer-token log probabilities and understanding the cross-entropy loss Implementing supervised training and tracking training and validation losses Evaluating checkpoints on MATH-500 and comparing distillation results Watch video 8 · Chapter 8 code Final words As you watch these lectures, I encourage you to pause occasionally and try a small experiment of your own if something interesting comes to mind. For example, feel free to change the sampling settings, inspect a few failed answers, or try variations of different ideas similar to the suggestions in the exercises. And if you would like the full written walkthrough, figures, and exercises alongside the videos, you can find Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) at Manning and Amazon . Thanks for reading and supporting Ahead of AI. I am taking a short break to regenerate, and I look forward to being back with the next round of LLM research articles next month. In the meantime, happy viewing and tinkering! 337 13 35 Share Discussion about this post Comments Restacks Bachu Adharsh Kumar 3d Liked by Sebastian Raschka, PhD Reasoning models explained from scratch is what students need. Do you think a small model can show real reasoning gains on a normal laptop? Reply Share 2 replies by Sebastian Raschka, PhD and others Shamik 2d Liked by Sebastian Raschka, PhD Thank you for the amazing content, as always. Now i have something to look forward to during the holiday season. Love the picture at the end. Happy regeneration. Reply Share 11 more comments... Top Latest Discussions No posts Ready for more? It won't fix your bug. It'll fix you. Every other tool hands you the answer; Nietzschian Debugger hands the question back. You paste your bug. It doesn't fix it. Instead, it: Challenges your assumptions about what's happening Forces you to confront the evidence you're avoiding Attacks the assumption you're proudest of — the one you stopped questioning Guides you to the fix yourself — your realization, not the AI's Why? AI is making developers weaker. Copy-paste from ChatGPT, ship, repeat. Nobody understands their own code anymore. Nietzschian Debugger forges stronger developers — through struggle, not shortcuts. This isn't anti-AI — it runs on Claude, on purpose. It's anti- outsourcing-your-thinking . Every other tool uses the model to hand you the answer; this one uses it to hand the question back. "He who has a why to debug can bear almost any how." Installation # Python 3.10+ pip install nietzschian-debugger nietzschian debug " your bug " No API key yet? See it in action first — no key, no cost: nietzschian demo Note: the current tool is the Python package above. The old npx nietzschian-debugger serves a stale pre-rewrite build — it has been deprecated in favour of the pip install. Requirements: Python >= 3.10 An Anthropic API key (BYOK) — or bring another model (OpenAI, Gemini, DeepSeek, …), or run a local Ollama model, which needs no key. See Models — set one up, switch any time . Setup Set your Anthropic API key: # Linux / macOS export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY= " sk-ant-... " # Windows (PowerShell) $env :ANTHROPIC_API_KEY = " sk-ant-... " # Windows (CMD) set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-... Quick Start # Start a debugging session (adaptive by default — it reads your state and shifts lens) nietzschian debug " My API returns 500 but only on Tuesdays " # Force a single lens instead of adapting nietzschian debug --lens socrates " My login endpoint fails randomly " nietzschian debug --lens zarathustra " Memory leak in production " # Point it at specific code nietzschian debug " Auth fails in ./src/middleware/auth.ts " # Interrogate your actual uncommitted changes (feeds the git diff as context) nietzschian debug --diff " tests started failing after my last change " # Use any model — Claude by default; or OpenAI, Gemini, DeepSeek, local Ollama… nietzschian debug --model ollama:llama3.1 " my function returns null sometimes " Models — set one up, switch any time Claude is the default and the sharpest experience. With ANTHROPIC_API_KEY set, every command just works with no flags. But the tool is model-agnostic — it speaks the OpenAI API, so almost any hosted or local model works too. Switching models The model is chosen per command with --model . There's no config to edit and no state to reset — you switch just by changing the flag, or drop it to return to Claude : nietzschian debug " my bug " # Claude (needs ANTHROPIC_API_KEY) nietzschian debug " my bug " --model openai:gpt-4o-mini # a hosted model nietzschian debug " my bug " --model ollama:llama3.1 # a local model, no key The flag isn't sticky — each run is independent. (There's no mid-session switch yet; to change model, re-run the command with a different --model .) Hosted models (bring your own key) Set the matching key, then select the model: export OPENAI_API_KEY=... # or GEMINI_API_KEY, DEEPSEEK_API_KEY, GROQ_API_KEY, … nietzschian debug --model openai:gpt-4o-mini " ... " nietzschian debug --model deepseek:deepseek-chat " ... " nietzschian debug --model gemini:gemini-1.5-flash " ... " Supported: openai, gemini, deepseek, groq, mistral, together, openrouter, xai — plus custom:<model> with NIETZSCHIAN_BASE_URL for any other OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Local models with Ollama (no key, no cost, offline) # 1. Install Ollama (https://ollama.com) and make sure it's running # 2. Pull a model once: ollama pull llama3.1 # 3. Add the provider deps once, then point the tool at it: pip install " nietzschian-debugger[providers] " nietzschian roast ./messy.py --model ollama:llama3.1 (LM Studio works the same way: --model lmstudio:<model> .) Which local model should I use? Different jobs reward different kinds of model — and the twist is that the best model for predict is the worst for roast : Command Best local model Why roast , debug a general chat model — llama3.1 , qwen3 built for prose and wit predict a coding model — qwen2.5-coder it wants a precise function call — exactly the dare A coding model asked to roast reaches for JSON instead of a joke; a chat model asked to predict is vaguer about the exact return value. Match the model to the job. Honest caveat: the "never give answers" discipline is sharpest on Claude . Smaller local models leak and over-ask more — the built-in validator and the roast/predict guards catch a lot of it, not all. Share a session Your sessions are made to be shared. Turn the last one into clean markdown: nietzschian share # most recent session, to your terminal nietzschian share -o run.md # or save it to a file Three Lenses — it picks, not you By default it adapts : each turn it reads where you are and shifts between three methods. You don't choose a difficulty — a confused developer can't diagnose their own state, so the tool reads you instead. Nietzsche is home; it shifts only on sustained signals, not twitchily, and the active lens shows in every turn header ( [Turn 3 · socrates] ). When you're… Lens What it does confused — you don't know what you mean socrates Relentless clarification. Defines your vague terms until a testable claim appears. The stingray, not a gentle mentor. avoiding — hiding in an assumption nietzsche The tuning fork. Taps the idol you're proudest of and listens for the hollow ring. defeated — ready to quit zarathustra Affirmation. Reframes the bug as the weight that makes you stronger, and will not let you quit. None of them is soft — adaptivity changes the angle of the blade, never sheathes it. To pin one lens instead of adapting: nietzschian debug --lens socrates " my bug " nietzschian debug --lens zarathustra " my bug " How a Session Looks $ nietzschian debug "login endpoint returns 403, but only for users who signed up before last week; new signups work; same code path; Node/Express" Nietzschian Debugger [Adaptive mode] [Turn 1 · nietzsche] You said "same code path" — but the data is screaming that something changed between last week and today. What is different about the user record itself between those who signed up before last week and those who signed up after? > I assumed the records were identical. Let me actually compare one. [Turn 2 · nietzsche] "Assumed." There is the word you built a week of debugging on. Stop assuming and read two rows side by side. What field exists on an old account that a new signup was never given? > ...the old ones carry a legacy role claim the new ones don't, and the auth middleware rejects any token without it. [Turn 3 · nietzsche] There it is. The bug was never in the code — it was in your certainty that "same code path" meant "same data." You stopped looking exactly where the difference lived. > found it Session Complete -- 3 questions to root cause (Solved) Your Debugging Profile: ┣ Assumption-checking ████████░░ strong ┣ Evidence-gathering ██████░░░░ moderate ┗ Root cause speed ████████░░ strong "Man is something that shall be overcome." -- Friedrich Nietzsche Or when you call a test "flaky": $ nietzschian debug "integration test passes locally but fails in CI — it's flaky, I just rerun until it's green" Nietzschian Debugger [Adaptive mode] [Turn 1 · nietzsche] "Flaky." The word you reach for when a test has found something true and you'd rather it hadn't. A test that fails one run in three isn't random — it's telling you something is ordered that you assumed was not. What does CI have, or do in a different order, that your machine does not? > idk, maybe the database isn't ready yet [Turn 2 · nietzsche] "Maybe" — you named a suspect and refused to question it in the same breath. A database that wasn't ready would throw a connection error, not a wrong answer. Unless your test is reading rows another test wrote. Do your tests share a database, and are they guaranteed to run in order? > ...they share one. locally they always run alphabetically [Turn 3 · nietzsche] There it is. "Flaky" was the mask on a race you refused to see — two tests fighting over the same rows, hidden on your machine by an accident of alphabetical ordering that CI parallelizes away. The test was never flaky. It was honest, and you were not. Will you isolate the data, or keep rolling the dice until they fall green? > oh. found it Session Complete -- 3 questions to root cause (Solved) Your Debugging Profile: ┣ Assumption-checking ███████░░░ strong ┣ Evidence-gathering █████░░░░░ moderate ┗ Root cause speed ████████░░ strong "No victor believes in chance." -- Friedrich Nietzsche Prove You Understand It — predict debug interrogates a bug. predict interrogates you : it dares you to say what one of your functions returns, then runs the code for the truth — never a model guessing (that can be confidently wrong). At the end it names the pattern in your misses, not a score. nietzschian predict ./parsers.py # 3 dares by default nietzschian predict ./parsers.py -n 5 # go five rounds $ nietzschian predict ./parsers.py Nietzschian Debugger [predict mode] 3 rounds — type 'quit' (or press Ctrl+C) to stop early. ── Round 1 of 3 ── You named it truncate, and now you believe it truncates. Sweet certainty. But look — you gave length a default of zero, and zero is a falsy little god that answers "if not length". So tell me, prophet: what does truncate("hello world") return? your prophecy > "" — it truncates to zero, so nothing Wrong, and gloriously so. "if not length" caught your zero and handed back the text untouched, before a single character was cut. You read the name and never the first line. The guard fired; your logic never ran. The truth, once run — it returned 'hello world'. ── Round 2 of 3 ── You wrote dedupe, and I can smell the doubt — most who write it reach for a set and let the order rot. Did you keep the order, or did you betray it? what does dedupe([3, 1, 2, 1, 3]) return? your prophecy > [3, 1, 2] Right — and not by luck. You kept the first sighting of each and dropped the echoes. Clean. There was no trap here; some things you simply know. The truth, once run — it returned [3, 1, 2]. ── Round 3 of 3 ── A tier function, a border drawn at one hundred. Borders are where confidence goes to die. Stand on the line itself and tell me which side claims you: what does shipping_tier(100) return? your prophecy > "freight" — 100 is the heavy tier Wrong. "weight > 100", and one hundred is not greater than one hundred. You stood ON the boundary and assumed it pulled you across; it let you fall back to 'parcel'. The strict > you typed yourself is the thing you forgot. The truth, once run — it returned 'parcel'. Proof of Understanding Two of three — and the two you missed were cut from the same cloth. You read functions by their name and their happy middle, and walk straight past the lines that quietly decide everything first: the falsy default that returns early, the strict > that owns its edge. You trust what the code is *for* over what it *says*. Read the guards before the gift — the boundary is not an afterthought, it is the whole argument. It runs your code in a separate process with a timeout — your own functions, called the way you'd call them. It only picks functions it can invoke with simple literal arguments, and a function that raises is a legitimate answer (predict that too). Roast Your Code — roast For when you don't want a question or a fix — you want the truth, fast and funny. Point it at your worst file; it reads the code's cowardice and laughs. Fixes nothing. nietzschian roast ./legacy/utils.py $ nietzschian roast ./legacy/utils.py 🔥 Nietzschian Roast A function named `helper` wrapping a bare `except: pass` — you built a room with no windows and called it tidy. The bug you're hiding from in there is the only honest thing you've written all week. "Not by wrath does one kill, but by laughter." — Thus Spoke Zarathustra Session Commands Command Effect solved or found it End session — you found the root cause I give up Get one lifeline question, then exit exit or quit Abandon session immediately Ctrl+C / Ctrl+D Force quit Features Refuses to Hand You the Fix — Every response is a question. It's built to withhold the answer, and a model-judge double-checks each reply to catch it when it slips. Proof of Understanding — predict dares you to say what your code returns, then runs it for the truth (never a model guessing) and names the pattern in your misses. Nietzschian Roast — roast reads your worst file and burns it down in one or two lines. Fixes nothing. Deeply shareable. Real Code Reading — Reference a file path and it reads YOUR actual code, not generic examples. --diff feeds it your uncommitted changes. Any Model, Even Local — Claude by default; or OpenAI, Gemini, DeepSeek, Groq, and more — or a local Ollama / LM Studio model with no key and no cost. Try With No Key — nietzschian demo runs a full scripted session so you can see it before committing a key. Shareable Sessions — nietzschian share exports a session as clean markdown you can post. Adaptive Lenses — it reads your state each turn and shifts between Socrates (when you're confused), Nietzsche (when you're avoiding), and Zarathustra (when you're defeated). You don't pick the difficulty; it reads you. Growth Score — Track your debugging skills across sessions with visual bar charts. Session History — All sessions saved locally in .nietzschian/sessions/ for trend tracking. Sliding Context — Long sessions don't crash; older turns are transparently summarized. Development # Clone and install git clone https://github.com/DilawarShafiq/nietzschian-debugger.git cd nietzschian-debugger pip install -e " .[dev] " # Run the test suite pytest # Run the CLI locally nietzschian debug " test problem " Tech Stack Python >= 3.10 Claude API via the Anthropic SDK Click for the CLI, Rich for the terminal UI pytest for testing License MIT About It won't fix your bug. It'll fix you. title: Solar power is becoming bigger than nuclear
body_text: 'It's offensively cheap': How solar power is quietly becoming bigger than nuclear Skip to content Watch Live British Broadcasting Corporation Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Home News US & Canada UK UK Politics England N. Ireland N. Ireland Politics Scotland Scotland Politics Wales Wales Politics Africa Asia China India Australia Europe Latin America Middle East In Pictures BBC InDepth BBC Verify Sport Business World of Business Technology of Business NYSE Opening Bell Technology Watch Documentaries Artificial Intelligence Intelligence Revolution AI v the Mind Tech Now Health Watch Documentaries Culture Watch Documentaries Film & TV Music Art & Design Style Books Entertainment News Arts Watch Documentaries Arts in Motion Travel Watch Documentaries Destinations Africa Antarctica Asia Australia and Pacific Caribbean & Bermuda Central America Europe Middle East North America South America World’s Table Culture & Experiences Adventures The SpeciaList To the Ends of the Earth Earth Watch Documentaries Science Natural Wonders Climate Solutions Sustainable Business Green Living Audio Podcast Categories Radio Audio FAQs Video Watch Documentaries BBC Maestro Discover the World Live Live News Live Sport Documentaries Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live 'It's offensively cheap': How solar power is quietly becoming bigger than nuclear 2 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Jocelyn Timperley Getty Images (Credit: Getty Images) After defying projections, solar's dramatic growth means it is now overtaking nuclear as a global power source. Here are seven reasons for solar's success, and where it might go from here. The world's solar power is crossing a threshold. A decade ago, it barely registered on a global scale, providing just 1% of the world's power. In 2026, it will almost certainly increase to 10% of power, and overtake nuclear, a mainstay of electricity since the late 1970s. Globally, solar electricity generation quietly overtook nuclear power (just) in 2025, according to statistics from UK-based energy think tank Ember . And BBC analysis of Ember data over the past 12 months up to September 2026 shows it clearly outstripping nuclear, producing 13% more power. "[Solar] generating more electricity than all the world's nuclear power plants is a pretty insane stat, for sure," says Dave Jones, co-founder of Ember. From China's vast arrays to a recent solar upsurge driven by escalating oil prices, the incredible rise of solar power has defied all projections. Here are seven ways it has become an apparently "unstoppable force" – and what the future looks like from here. 1. An underestimated force "Solar is now the engine of the power transition," says Jan Rosenow, a professor of energy and climate policy at the University of Oxford in the UK. Solar has become the fastest-growing source of new electricity in history , and by far the largest source of new electricity globally. In 2025, it met three-quarters of the growth in the world's demand for electricity, overtaking wind power generation (wind power is also growing, just a little more slowly). That's where solar's going, to not just be king of electricity, but king of energy – Dave Jones "It wasn't expected," says Rosenow. Mainstream projections, he says, have underestimated solar year after year . Outlooks such as those from the International Energy Agency (IEA), an influential intergovernmental organisation based in Paris, "assumed linear growth and slowly falling costs, and got both wrong". Over 2026, multiple sources indicate solar electricity generation will almost certainly far exceed nuclear globally. Nuclear's electricity generation has remained more or less constant since 2000, while solar's has increased some 2,700-fold. Ember/ BBC Ember data shows solar electricity generation narrowly surpassing nuclear in 2025. In 2026, it will almost certainly well exceed it (Credit: Ember/BBC) 2. 'Offensively cheap' Solar, a mature technology for some 15 years now, became the cheapest electricity in history in 2020. Since then, solar has scaled, efficiency has risen, and the amount of silicon and silver used in panels has gone down, leading prices to fall yet further , says Jones. "Massive Chinese manufacturing scale and current overcapacity have pushed module prices to record lows," says Rosenow. In particular, a large fall in the price of panels in 2023-24 pushed us into the current era of what Jones calls "offensively cheap" solar. "A panel in itself is just so unbelievably cheap," he says. "It's well under $100 (£75)… and that's going to keep you generating electricity for 30, 40 years without any input at all." Of course, it's not just in purely economic terms that solar is bringing down costs. Researchers have calculated the US's rising wind and solar generation brought it $249bn (£186bn) in climate and health benefits between 2019 and 2022 . 3. Global uptake China is still the world's biggest solar power by far but is by no means the only player. Despite the US imposing a variety of tariffs on solar , it remains the second country when it comes to installations, which are still skyrocketing – especially in states won by President Trump in 2024 . In fact, the US now has enough solar to power more than one-third of its households . "Tariffs and other federal policies that constrain renewable energy growth are certainly expected to raise costs and slow expansion relative to what we otherwise would have seen," says Alicia Zhao, an expert in US mitigation pathways at the University of Maryland. "However, economics are a key part of why solar has been able to grow so quickly. Even with rising costs, solar is still one of the cheapest sources of new power in the US. And it is getting built regardless of political lines ." Getty Images China's internal solar boom is now slowing down, but its cheap solar exports to other countries are still increasing (Credit: Getty Images) India, meanwhile, is moving away from fossil fuels far faster than China did, and new solar has met 60% of its rise in power demand in the past two years. In Australia, over four million homes now have rooftop solar: well over a third of all households. 4. Unreliable fossil fuels Countries like Pakistan and Lebanon have also begun installing solar at breakneck speeds , while across Africa countries are installing some 100,000 solar panels per day. In many places, escalating diesel prices, driven by the Russia-Ukraine conflict and US-Israel war with Iran , has swung the cost needle yet further in solar's favour. This is especially the case in many African countries where home diesel generators are a mainstay due to unreliable grids. Rooftop solar panels, nearly all of them imported from China, have now taken off as an alternative. Ethiopia has even banned the import of petrol and diesel cars in a bid to tackle oil dependency and pollution, says Jones. Solar is also rapidly providing new electricity where fossil-based grids can't keep up with demand. Pakistan, for example, has become a surprising poster child for the solar revolution due to its extraordinarily rapid rise in installations . In 2019, solar provided less than 2% of its electricity; now it's 24%, driven by costly, unreliable grid electricity combined and cheap solar imports from China. "What's really incredible in Pakistan is… generally most of the solar boom has been out of people's pockets," says Jones. "People can afford it, without needing to take out loans." A similar story has been seen in several other "sun belt" countries, from Lebanon to Nigeria . "[Solar] lets households act without waiting for governments or utilities," says Rosenow. "In uncertain times, that speed and independence is extremely valuable." 5. Battery revolution Solar power, of course, can only be produced during the day when the sun is shining. To turn it into electricity that can be dispatched at any time, it needs to be paired with batteries. Fortunately, batteries have been having their own cost revolution , transforming their ability to support the solar rollout. "Solar plus storage is now routinely cheaper than new fossil plants in sunny regions," says Rosenow. "Batteries have largely solved the daily problem of shifting midday sun into the evening." Alamy Solar has gone from Pakistan's fifth-largest electricity source in 2023 to its largest in 2025, says Rosenow (Credit: Alamy) In California, for example, solar and batteries met on average over a quarter of electricity demand from 19:00-21:00 (the evening peak) over the first half of 2026. US states such as Vermont are now rolling out grid-integrated systems of home batteries, often paired with solar. Barriers still remain for longer-term storage of solar across seasons, cloudy periods and monsoon seasons, though, both Rosenow and Jones say. It means the integration of solar into the wider electricity system still matters, says Rosenow. 6. Electrify everything Solar is seen as a key part of the push towards electrification , reducing fossil fuel use in areas that previously didn't use electricity, such as via electric cars. Electrification has been chosen as a major theme at this year's UN climate talks in Turkey . "That's where solar's going, to not just be king of electricity, but king of energy," says Jones. Still, it all requires a plan, Julia Souder, chief executive of the Long Duration Energy Storage Council, a global executive-led non-profit established at COP26, warned recently . "There is an inherent danger in uncontrolled electrification, and adding massive new loads without built-in flexibility creates a fragile system," she wrote in a blog for international policy network Ren21. "Electrification is not automatically resilient." The limits on solar are now grids, storage and how fast we electrify demand, says Rosenow – not panels or cost. "The bigger question is no longer whether solar grows but whether our power systems and institutions can keep up." In the US, data centres and electrification mean power demand is growing for the first time in decades, says Zhao, with energy security a national priority . "Renewables already make up over 90% of new capacity in the US," she says. "This need for secure, quickly deployable electricity could create a critical opportunity for [further] renewable energy growth even without support from the current federal government." 7. Expanding tech In the past few years, plug-in panels (or "balcony solar"), have started spreading rapidly in Germany . These generate less electricity than rooftop panels but feed it directly into homes via a standard socket. They have now been approved in several other countries and US states including California . Meanwhile, agrivoltaics, which combines food production and solar panels, is being touted as a solution to concerns in some areas about the land use of solar. Getty Images In Kentucky, US, a solar ranch pays a local farmer to graze his sheep among its solar panels, producing pasture-fed meat while keeping grass and weeds down (Credit: Getty Images) Other technologies from floating and "mirror" solar plants to perovskite panels and solar windows could all see growth in coming years. What's next for solar In 2026, the world's solar capacity will go on rising, but the rate of expansion may slow down for the first time ever, says Jones. This is down to China: last summer, it changed its regime for managing and supporting new solar installations , leading to a burst of installations in 2025 to fall under the old price regime. Elsewhere, it's a different picture. "If you exclude China, there's more panels being installed this year than last year," says Jones. By 2030, the IEA thinks solar power generation will have reached double that of 2025's levels, with solar overtaking hydro to become the world's third-largest electricity source . "Wherever grid power is costly and unreliable, the economics keep pulling people towards solar," says Rosenow. "There is one caveat: if Chinese solar panels are difficult to import this will not happen at speed." More like this: • The US state replacing power plants with home batteries • The dream of beaming solar energy from orbit • Perovskite: The 'wonder material' that could transform solar There has been a lot of bad news about the climate recently. It's now incredibly likely the 1.5C global limit set in Paris in 2015 will be breached, the world is seeing rising climate impacts and is edging towards several climate tipping points this century. But the solar success story shows we are also making progress in ways that were never anticipated. A decade ago, "no one was getting close to expecting that to happen", says Jones, noting that the growth in clean electricity has directly translated to fewer coal plants being built. "Now, worst cases [of climate change] are somewhere between 2-3C of warming, rather than 4C of warming." -- For essential climate news and hopeful developments to your inbox, sign up to the Future Earth newsletter, while The Essential List delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights twice a week. Oldest GUI application that still runs on Windows 11
body_text: Oldest GUI application that still runs on Windows 11 Â· enlyth enlyth . posts tags rss Oldest GUI application that still runs on Windows 11 26 October 2026 Â· 2 min read #windows #gui Early investigation For a while Iâve been wondering about a silly question, which is, whatâs the oldest application with a GUI that will still run on Windows 11 without modifications or emulation. Given Windowsâ excellent backwards compatibility, I expected the answer to be something impressively old. Sadly, Windows 11 canât run 16-bit Windows programs by itself, because 64-bit Windows has no NTVDM , so weâre going to have to find something from the early NT era. I remember asking this question a while ago on an anonymous forum, where someone pointed me to Win32s , and suggested to find an early release version of it with FREECELL.exe . So I did exactly that, and lo and behold, FREECELL.EXE with a date modified of 22-Feb-93 running and fully playable, without any changes on the latest version of Windows 11: At the time of this post, thatâs a 33 years and 8 months old application, which is impressively almost as old as me. So I kinda thought âcoolâ, considered this a solved mystery and forgot about it shortly afterwards. But for some reason, this question popped into my mind again lately and this time I decided to dig deeper to see if I can find something older. Further efforts Digging through old Windows versions on the Internet Archive, I found some early NT 3.1 pre-release versions that seemed promising, but the main issue seemed to be either incompatibility with todayâs executable format or API changes that came later in development. The earliest 1991 versions used a draft PE format not compatible with modern Windows, and builds up to mid-1992 assumed the cdecl calling convention instead of stdcall for Windows API calls, so arguments would get removed twice, as such: push hwnd ; 4 bytes of args call [ShowWindow] ; Win11 ShowWindow is stdcall, ends with "ret 4" and removes them add esp, 4 ; the 1992 caller removes them again Which would understandably cause the program to crash. There was one application that caught my eye though, from Build 347, and that was CDPLAYER.EXE , linked on 16-Nov-1992 . By then the calling convention was fixed, but the other programs in that build crash in their bundled C runtime. CDPLAYER.EXE avoids that by using the systemâs crtdll.dll , and Windows 11 still ships a crtdll.dll in SysWOW64 . If you start the program, you get something like this: That is because, duh, my computer doesnât have a CD-ROM drive. But you can use a small DLL ( cdemu.dll ) to emulate one with some fake audio data and actually get it to play audio: Pretty cool for a program thatâs almost 34 years old! What if we cheat? So earlier I mentioned that 16-bit programs are out of the picture because they are no longer supported. But if you want, you can use something like otvdm to run older Windows applications. Behold, a fully playable version of REVERSI.EXE dated 15-Nov-1985 running on Windows 11, taken from Windows 1.01: And although using otvdm does feel like cheating, I thought it was cool enough to include in this post.
