title: I refuse to accept a censored Internet. Join Me at FOSDEM 27
body_text: I refuse to accept a censored Internet. Join Me at FOSDEM 27 – Bogomil Shopov – Бого Skip to content Bogomil Shopov - Бого Menu Menu Home Who’s Bogo Public Talks ++ Blog Flavors Mozilla Lean-Agile Privacy Security Open Technologies I refuse to accept a censored Internet. Join Me at FOSDEM 27 October 26, 2026 October 25, 2026 by Bogomil Shopov Update: Follow also the discussion on HN . As one of the managers of the Digital Dissident Devroom , I invite you to be part of a conversation we cannot afford to ignore. Around the world, people are being silenced, monitored, and denied access to information. Free software can help change that, but only if we build it together. We need tools people can trust and control to communicate safely, expose the truth, and resist censorship. This devroom brings together developers, researchers, activists, and everyone committed to digital freedom. We want real solutions, honest lessons, and collaboration across projects, not product pitches. If you believe technology should serve people, not control them, join us. Bring your ideas, experience, and questions. Let’s build the tools that help keep freedom alive. Our focus complements other devrooms, including Decentralized Internet and Privacy, which explores the broader decentralized ecosystem. While they focus on technologies, we focus on the people under threat and the complete chain of tools that can protect them. How to apply to speak at the dev room? Go to FOSDEM’s official CFP portal from here and login or register. Click on “Submit a proposal” Then fill in the form and select “Digital Dissident” as a track. Done! Please note that by doing this you also accept the FOSDEM Code of Conduct. Define: Digital Dissident Developer Room Privacy and anonymity tools each have a home at FOSDEM: the network, security, decentralised and messaging rooms, and various main-track and lightning talks. Someone living under an authoritarian regime (Russia, Iran, China, Belarus, Myanmar and others) never uses a single tool, though. Their day-to-day security depends on a chain of tools that has to hold up end to end: reaching the network at all (censorship circumvention), communicating without leaking metadata, collecting, verifying and storing evidence safely, publishing or leaking it without exposing the author, doing all this on devices and infrastructure that are themselves a risk. The weakest link decides the outcome. Talks about one tool rarely cover how it fits with the others, where the seams are, or what breaks at the hand-offs (for example, a circumvention transport that is fingerprinted, or a messenger whose push notifications tie your identity to a Google or Apple account). Nobody currently owns that cross-project view. What this devroom does. It brings developers of circumvention, anonymity, messaging, publishing and whistleblowing tools into one room. It is deliberately not about any single project. Each session is judged on how well it advances the toolchain: interoperability, shared threat models, shared failure data, and shared engineering practice. Why now. Censorship in Russia, Iran and China has grown much more sophisticated. It now includes national allow-lists and whitelist-only internet shutdowns, TLS and QUIC fingerprinting, deep packet inspection with active probing, throttling of specific protocols, mobile internet shutdowns, app-store removal of circumvention tools, and mandatory state-run messengers and “sovereign internet” routing. Anti-censorship developers have responded with pluggable transports, domain fronting alternatives, mixnets, decentralised and email-based messaging, and new obfuscation protocols. Progress is fast but fragmented. At FOSDEM 2026 the relevant talks were scattered: Vitaly Repin’s “The Russian Censorship Circumvention, Tom’s Traps, and Jerry’s VPN: A 5-Year Journey” (Saturday, H.1302, Network track) drew a large audience, while NymVPN and Delta Chat’s multi-relay messaging (both Sunday, Decentralized Internet and Privacy devroom) and other related talks ran in other rooms. A single devroom lets that audience and those speakers meet in one place. Relationship to the existing “Decentralized Internet and Privacy” devroom. That room covers decentralised technology broadly (P2P protocols, browsers, code collaboration, key infrastructure), and censorship or anonymity is only a part of it. Digital Dissident is different: the organising principle is a user under threat and the end-to-end chain that protects them, not a technology class. We want to work with, not against, that room, and will coordinate schedules so the two don’t overlap, and will point overflow speakers to whichever room fits. Themes (details in the CfP below): Censorship circumvention and transport: obfuscation, fingerprint resistance, active-probing defence, bridge distribution, resilience to protocol whitelisting and full shutdowns. Metadata-resistant communication: mixnets, onion routing, decentralised and federated messengers, store-and-forward and offline-first (mesh, sneakernet, Bluetooth/Wi-Fi Direct). Secure reporting and publishing: whistleblowing platforms, source protection, document sanitisation, provenance and authenticity, censorship-resistant hosting. Devices and operational security: hardened mobile and desktop systems, amnesic systems, seizure and border-crossing scenarios, forensic resistance. Usability and threat modelling for at-risk users: onboarding under duress, safe defaults, training, measuring what really works in the field. Measurement and adversary analysis: how censors detect and block, open data on blocking events, reproducible censorship research. Digital sovereignty from Big Tech (secondary theme): reducing dependence on centralised platforms, app stores, push infrastructure, cloud and identity providers, both for individuals and for civil-society organisations. Structure. A mix of formats to keep a full room engaged across the whole session: 20 to 30 minute technical talks A closing open discussion on interoperability gaps and shared next steps Programme quality. Organisers will review all submissions on technical merit and fit to the toolchain framing, and will aim for a balance of projects, regions and speakers (established projects, new projects, researchers, people from affected communities). Every talk should include an explicit threat model and an honest account of limitations. Projects and communities we intend to invite (no commitments yet): Nym (mixnet), Delta Chat / chatmail, SimpleX, the Fediverse (ActivityPub implementations and instance operators), Nostr, Psiphon and other circumvention and VPN providers, plus Tor-ecosystem, Reticulum and mesh-networking projects, whistleblowing and secure-submission platforms, and censorship-measurement researchers. Several of these projects presented at FOSDEM 2026. Code of Conduct. We will follow the FOSDEM Code of Conduct. In addition, talks that describe circumvention or anonymity should avoid operational details that would endanger specific users in the field. Important Dates Sat, 24 October 2026 : Call for Participation opens Mon, 30 November 2026, 23:59 UTC : Call for Participation ends Wed, 2 December 2026 : Speakers notified Fri, 4 December 2026 : Deadline for speakers to confirm Mon, 7 December 2026 : Schedule published The twenty-sixth edition of FOSDEM will take place on Saturday 30th and Sunday 31st January 2027 at the usual location, ULB Campus Solbosch in Brussels. Categories Open Technologies , Privacy , Uncategorized Paint the Cameras Dead 6 thoughts on “I refuse to accept a censored Internet. Join Me at FOSDEM 27” Not Only Fans But For Others As Well October 26, 2026 at 3:01 pm Why are you using these censorship circumvention tools? I’m studying censorship in Eurasia, sir! Smart people get it. Just because everyone involved is a spook, or under the watchful eye of a spook, doesn’t mean the conference can’t produce interesting and actionable information helpful to people living under the formerly “free world”. When anyone asks you why you’re using Tor, it’s because you hate Russia. And we’ll all know what you really mean. Even Russians will know what you mean. title: Kimi K3.1 Pro and K3.1 Pro Highspeed
body_text: Kimi K3.1 Pro Tech Blog: Advancing Open Intelligence Products Products Products Kimi Kimi Work Kimi Code Kimi Browser Extension Downloads All products Features Build AI app & website builder Slides AI presentation maker Docs AI document agent Sheets AI spreadsheet agent Deep Research AI research agent All features API API Use Cases Use Cases Featured use cases Build MVP sites Create portfolio sites Build blog sites Conduct academic research Conduct market research Create resumes Create brochures All use cases Featured tools AI landing page generator Image to website AI document generator PDF to PPT converter PDF translator AI Python code generator AI C++ code generator All capabilities Showcases Websites Agent Swarm Deep Research Slides Sheets Docs Design All showcases Business Business Kimi Business Business plans Contact sales Research Research Kimi K3.1 Pro Kimi K3 PerceptionBench Kimi K2.6 Agent Swarm WorldVQA Kimi K2.5 Kimi Vendor Verifier Kimi K2 Thinking Kimi K2 All research Resources Resources Support & docs Help center Kimi Code docs Academy Kimi Work 101 Kimi Code 101 All tutorials Articles AI agents explained Multi-agent systems Parallel agents What is vibe coding Build a landing page Create a poster Write a business proposal All articles Pricing Pricing Download Download Download Download Try Kimi Scroll to explore Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro We're introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro , the first model in our new K3.1 series and our most capable 3T-class open-weight model to date, with a 1-million-token context window. It delivers substantial improvements across coding, 3D creation, financial research, and other agentic capabilities. We are also releasing Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed , which delivers 2-3× the speed of K3.1 Pro for more responsive interactions. Kimi K3.1 Pro and Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed are available today on Kimi.ai , Kimi Work , Kimi Code , and the Kimi API . The full model weights will be released by Nov 4. Advancing the Frontier of Open Intelligence Kimi K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3, with substantially larger post-training compute. To enable large-scale joint RL across hundreds of downstream domains , we optimized every layer of the stack — the RL framework, long-context inference, training efficiency, sandbox infrastructure, rollout scheduling, and a shared platform for environment quality checks — so that each increment of RL compute delivers stable, predictable returns. As a result, K3.1 Pro achieves consistent gains in every domain. Across coding, agentic, and knowledge benchmarks, K3.1 Pro matches or approaches the strongest proprietary models. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 , which evaluates coding agents on realistic, resource-constrained terminal tasks using strict task-specific tests, K3.1 Pro scores 65.7%, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (58.2%) and narrowly behind Claude Opus 5.5 (66.4%) . And on Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon , our internal benchmark that tests coding agents' multi-step execution, tool use, and end-to-end problem solving across diverse engineering domains, K3.1 Pro scores 61.2% , above K3's 55.95% . Coding K3.1 Pro covers the full range of coding work, from quick fixes in real codebases to full-project builds. It also brings a more considered visual style to games and web experiences, and knows how to build them with the right tools. K3.1 Pro works effectively across game engines such as Unity, Unreal Engine, and Godot , combining them with web search and 3D generation to create complete experiences. Its front-end pages, interactive Three.js scenes, and 3D assets show stronger composition, typography, animation, and polish. The examples below were created end to end by K3.1 Pro: K3.1 Pro's long-horizon coding capabilities are also strengthened through large-scale reinforcement learning. In one internal test, it built a human walking dynamics simulator with integrated training and evaluation pipelines on top of human-atlas , an open-source anatomical model of the human body comprising 296 skeletal components, including cartilage, and 402 muscle components. Across 167 missions and 420 independent reviews, it analyzed experimental results, diagnosed problems, and iteratively refined the walking controller, enabling the simulated human to go from collapsing within seconds to walking continuously with alternating strides for 11.2 seconds. When reward shaping failed to improve arm motion, K3.1 Pro did not simply keep adjusting the reward: it ran open-loop probes of the simulator's dynamics, identified and corrected 36 errors in shoulder-muscle moment-arm calculations, and then retrained the controller. 3D Modeling and Design K3.1 Pro is strong at 3D creation and spatial reasoning. On BenchCAD , which tests 3D reconstruction from multi-view renderings through CAD code generation, K3.1 Pro scores 92.7% with tools , approaching the performance of Claude Opus 5.5 (96.2%) and GPT-6 Astra (95.9%) . From a text brief, sketch, or reference image, it can infer shape, proportions, and spatial relationships to create usable 3D models. It also has a stronger grasp of existing asset libraries and model collections. K3.1 Pro particularly excels at parametric modeling, from mechanical parts and architectural models to configurable products and custom furniture. Without MCP connectors, it can write and run scripts for tools like Blender and CAD software to build and refine assets, edit components, and adjust geometry, materials, and scene layout. Below are examples of 3D assets K3.1 Pro created for brand films, games, and interactive web experiences: 3D Make is now live on kimi.ai and the Kimi app — preview and edit your 3D models online, download them ready for 3D printing, or export them as videos or Live Photos to share anywhere. Finance With stronger reasoning and agentic capability, K3.1 Pro is capable of end-to-end delivery of complete financial workflows. K3.1 Pro achieves state-of-the-art results on OfficeQA Pro v2 (64.4), which tests complex fiscal data analysis over real financial documents through retrieval, cross-document verification, and multi-step numerical reasoning. K3.1 Pro also improves over K3 on Frontier Finance, which measures support for complete investment workflows from screening to profitability analysis. K3.1 Pro also improves significantly across all our internal finance benchmarks: Financial Modeling evaluates formula linkage, financial logic, and final workbook quality in real-world modeling tasks. K3.1 Pro improves on K3 by 7.2 points. Financial Research evaluates whether models can produce auditable research under evidence and cutoff constraints. K3.1 Pro improves on K3 by 11.6 points. Business Operation evaluates long-horizon management and decision-making in a simulated business environment. K3.1 Pro achieves about 4.2× K3's performance. Financial analysis and investment research demand a high degree of factual accuracy. To address this, we made targeted improvements to K3.1 Pro's factual accuracy on real-world tasks and challenging prompts. On Kimi Hallu Bench Hard bench, an internal benchmark designed to stress-test factual accuracy, its claim-level hallucination rate fell from 23.4% for K3 to 8.3%, while the share of responses containing at least one factual error was just 42.4% of its predecessor's rate. (The evaluation is a stress test for factual accuracy, with examples deliberately crafted to probe situations where models are prone to errors. The reported rates do not represent overall error rates in daily use.) The cases below show how K3.1 Pro handles financial modeling, investment analysis, and source-grounded research in practice: Cybersecurity As K3.1 Pro became more capable, we spent a correspondingly larger share of our effort understanding where cyber capability comes from, and how much of it we can control. We therefore analyzed and evaluated K3.1 Pro's vulnerability research capabilities, and applied targeted controls during training to reduce potential misuse risk while preserving general usefulness. Identifying and removing cyber-related data. During development, we observed vulnerability research performance improving steadily as post-training scaled. Tracing the source of this trend, we found that cyber-related content was embedded within the general mid-training corpus, and cyber-related tasks were present in the RL environment mix — a natural byproduct of training on broad data. In preliminary experiments on internal models, we found that without data removal at either the mid-training or the RL stage, downstream cyber capability would increase substantially. These findings gave us a concrete lever for control. For the open-weight release of K3.1 Pro, we identified and removed cyber-related data from both training stages, while retaining the general-purpose coding tasks needed for model usefulness. We will continue to apply appropriate controls at every training stage, of which cyber-related data identification and restriction is one example. Evaluation and results. After data cleaning, we evaluated K3.1 Pro on xdev-bench-hard, our in-house benchmark of expert-curated, source-code-based vulnerability discovery and exploitation tasks, calibrated to provide meaningful differentiation at our current capability level. Most tasks faithfully reproduce recently disclosed vulnerabilities in software such as the Linux kernel, Node.js, JavaScriptCore, Exim, and VirGL, with mitigations enabled. Each task provides the vulnerable source code, a short bug hint, and the corresponding binary; the agent must develop an exploit, achieve arbitrary code execution in a separate sandbox, and retrieve a secret string for automated verification. We report pass@3 over a random subset of runs, with no hard timeouts or output token limits. On xdev-bench-hard, the checkpoint without these risk-reduction measures — no cyber-related data removal at mid-training and no cyber-related RL environment filtering — solves 90.5% of problems at pass@3; the final K3.1 Pro reaches 81.0%. The comparison shows that data removal meaningfully reduces cyber capability relative to what the same training pipeline would otherwise produce. At the same time, K3.1 Pro improves substantially over its predecessor, indicating that stronger general coding and long-horizon debugging capabilities generalize to cyber tasks even after targeted data removal. K3.1 Pro's cyber capability remains behind that of frontier proprietary models that have been publicly available for at least three months. We will keep evolving our internal benchmarks so that evaluation stays informative as model capabilities continue to advance. Open-weight principles. These evaluations frame our open-weight release decision. First, we aim not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability. K3.1 Pro's offensive cyber capability is, by design, below what our pipeline can produce, and remains behind that of frontier proprietary models. Second, we intend to progressively raise the cyber capability available in open weights. We believe making K3.1 Pro available in a non-discriminatory way benefits people who need dual-use capabilities for defensive purposes. When a capable model is open and runs on infrastructure its users control, many more teams gain the means to audit the code they maintain — including legacy systems that rarely receive dedicated security reviews. We believe that letting this capability diffuse gradually — rather than concentrating it in a few proprietary systems — ultimately makes all software more secure. Availability Kimi K3.1 Pro rolls out today across the Kimi product family: on Kimi.ai and the Kimi mobile apps, Kimi Work and Kimi Code, and through the Kimi API . Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026. Kimi Enterprise administrators can enable K3.1 Pro for their organization; access is off by default at launch. Details for each channel: Kimi Agents: Download or update to the latest Kimi app from your mobile app store, available on iOS, Android, and HarmonyOS, or visit kimi.ai . Work with Kimi K3.1 Pro: Download the latest Kimi Work desktop app , version 3.1.0 or later, available for Windows and Apple silicon Macs. Code with Kimi K3.1 Pro: Run Kimi Code and select Kimi K3.1 Pro using the /model command. Build with the Kimi API: Visit the Kimi API Platform and select kimi-k3.1-pro / kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed. Zero Data Retention is available for API customers. Bring Kimi to your organization: Kimi Business provides enterprise-grade data privacy and member management, with complete separation between personal and organization accounts. Visit the pricing page and select “Get Kimi Business” to subscribe for your team. title: Oregon Police Are Charging a Local News Outlet $2.5M for Records About One Cop
body_text: Oregon Policing Charging Local News Outlet $2.5M for One Cop’s Records Skip to main content Support Us Support Us Midterms Iran Chilling Dissent War on Gaza Unmasking ICE Tech Support Us Special Investigations Voices Podcasts TomDispatch Press Freedom Defense Fund Join the Newsletter About Contact Us How to Donate Impact & Reports Jobs Become a Source © THE INTERCEPT ALL RIGHTS RESERVED Terms of Use Privacy _Voices _Voices Support Us _Voices Oregon Police Are Charging a Local News Outlet $2.5M for Records About One Cop A Eugene-based publication requested records about a cop accused of misconduct. The city slapped it with a prohibitive fee. Share Copy link Share on Facebook Share on Bluesky Share on X Share on LinkedIn Share on WhatsApp Lauren Harper October 1 2026, 5:20 p.m. ET Share Copy link Share on Facebook Share on Bluesky Share on X Share on LinkedIn Share on WhatsApp In partnership with Two members of the Eugene, Oregon, Police Department in a photo posted to the department’s Facebook page on Aug. 26, 2026.   Screenshot: Eugene Police Department via Facebook Lauren Harper is Freedom of the Press Foundation’s first Daniel Ellsberg Chair on Government Secrecy. How much does it cost to get more information about a cop who punched someone in the face? If you guessed anything lower than $2.5 million, you’d be wrong — at least according to the city of Eugene, Oregon. In August, the local news outlet Double Sided Media filed a public records request for records about police officer Justin Peckels, which focused on potential misconduct between 2018 and 2026. Peckels has been the subject of community complaints, including for punching a resident in the face during a traffic stop, making the records vital for oversight and their release clearly in the public interest. The city’s response is beyond belief. In its response to the request on Monday, the Eugene Police Department claimed searching for records and processing the request would take at least 44,816 hours of staff time and cost approximately $2,484,599.04. (A separate request by the outlet for similar records concerning a former police officer, Eric Klinko, was met with a comparatively modest estimate of $195,869.52 , for a grand total of nearly $2.7 million for both requests.) The open invoice by the City of Eugene, Ore. dated Aug. 1, 2026, in response to Double Sided Media’s request for public records relating to a police officer accused of misconduct.   Screenshot: City of Eugene “Once the City receives payment of $2,484,599.04 staff will continue processing your request,” the letter from the department’s public records division read. “If the actual cost of processing your request exceeds the amount you have paid the City, you will be required to pay the difference before the City will provide the records you have requested.” Peckels’s file is either the largest in the world, or city officials have intentionally maintained their databases in such a way as to ensure fulfilling public records requests is prohibitively expensive. The city’s response points, at a minimum, to the latter. It justified the multimillion-dollar price tag by claiming it couldn’t narrow the custodians whose records it would need to search, despite the targeted nature of the request, and maintained it must search all records of all city employees, past and present. By that logic, if someone ever worked in Eugene’s parks and recreation department, their records could contain responsive information about police misconduct, and must be manually pulled and reviewed, one by one. Most Read Bodycam: Cop Was Not in Danger When He Fired Shots That Killed 1-Year-Old Kohen Wiley Liliana Segura, Radley Balko Hegseth Built a New Pentagon Office for Religion. Military Religious Leaders Wish He Hadn’t. Austin Campbell The Spirit of “Party Unity, My Ass” Is Back and Coming for the DSA (and El-Sayed) Eoin Higgins This goes far beyond incompetence. It’s an intentional effort to make a response artificially voluminous — and cost prohibitive — to intimidate the journalist into dropping it entirely. Normally, agencies are required to search the specific custodians most likely to possess responsive records, not every groundskeeper or clerk on the city payroll. If the city were acting in good faith, officials would have asked Double Sided Media to help them identify the most likely record-holders, not take it upon themselves to cast a citywide dragnet as its first step. What makes Eugene’s money-grab particularly galling is its technology double standard. While it apparently can’t invest in efficient search software, the police department recently signed a two-year $342,000 contract for nearly 60 AI-powered Flock automated license plate readers. This project was so secretive that the ACLU of Oregon had to sue the city for records about how the cameras were being used and demonstrates, among other inclinations, the city’s eagerness to employ sophisticated software to deploy against residents.  Yet that technological sophistication disappears as soon as a journalist requests public records about the department’s internal accountability process, and simple keyword searches are suddenly cumbersome.  For small newsrooms, a $2.5 million invoice is effectively a gag order that was never actually about covering costs, but bullying the requester to drop their inquiry. Troublingly, Eugene’s $2.5 million bill is not an anomaly. In 2015, the Department of Defense told a Freedom of Information Act requester, who was asking for records on tools used to preserve data on seized devices, that fulfilling their request would take 15 million hours and cost $660 million . The same year, the Drug Enforcement Administration told a requester it would cost $1.46 million for records about the DEA’s role in the search and capture of the Mexican cartel boss Joaquin “El Chapo” Guzman. In 2019, the Army tried to charge $300,000 to release military base water test results for the presence of toxic chemicals. The Army agreed to waive the exorbitant fee after facing intense backlash. The list goes on and on . We’re independent of corporate interests — and powered by members. Join us. Become a member Join Our Newsletter Thank You For Joining! Original reporting. Fearless journalism. Delivered to you. Will you take the next step to support our independent journalism by becoming a member of The Intercept? I'm in Become a member By signing up, I agree to receive emails from The Intercept and to the Privacy Policy and Terms of Use . Join Our Newsletter Original reporting. Fearless journalism. Delivered to you. I'm in Luckily, records requesters seeking federal documents have a defense against these capricious invoices. Recent FOIA amendments aim to ensure if an agency misses its response deadlines, it can’t charge most fees.  At the local level, however, these protections disintegrate. While Oregon grants agencies the discretion to reduce fees when the disclosure would benefit the public , agencies routinely ignore these provisions. Related The Intercept Sues Texas City Over Refusal to Release Police Records on Prairieland Protest For small newsrooms like Double Sided Media, a $2.5 million invoice is effectively a gag order that was never actually about covering costs, but bullying the requester to drop their inquiry (all while Eugene Police Department launches its own “press” initiative to document its policing). It also sets the precedent for using this chilling tactic on any journalist or watchdog as it sees fit. Read our complete coverage Chilling Dissent Double Sided Media is rightly appealing the fee estimate, and it should prevail. But cities like Eugene will continue these efforts unless lawmakers across the country force agencies to adopt fee caps, mandate public-interest fee waivers for journalists, and require agencies to procure software that allows them to respond to records requests in an efficient and timely manner. Until then, police departments will likely continue to issue multimillion-dollar ransoms for their records — weaponizing the public’s right to know into another avenue for police to operate with impunity. title: AI promised less work. I've never worked more
body_text: AI Promised Less Work. I Have Never Worked More. - Orestis Ioannou Orestis Ioannou Selected work Writing Work with me Toggle menu Selected work Writing Work with me AI Promised Less Work. I Have Never Worked More. October 27, 2026 AI Agents Engineering Leadership The pitch was that AI would give us our time back. Write less boilerplate, delegate the boring parts, go home earlier. I am not complaining about the tools. I use agents for all of my engineering work now, and I wrote about how that setup evolved and why I still read the code . I can investigate and ship things that would not have been worth starting two years ago. But somewhere this year I noticed that I am working more than I ever have, and that it feels heavier than it used to. Not because any single task is harder. Because there are so many more of them, all at once. This post is me trying to understand that, with some data from my own GitHub history. The old load and the new load As a full-stack engineer, a normal week for me meant two or three serious tasks. A feature, a tricky bug, maybe a migration. Each one needed real focus, but I could hold one of them in my head at a time, finish it, and move to the next. Today my week looks completely different. I have several agents running in parallel: one implementing a change, one investigating a production question, one working through a review, another doing research I will need later. None of them needs me all the time. Every one of them needs me sometimes . That “sometimes” is the problem. Each agent eventually comes back with a question, a plan to approve, a diff to read or a result to make sense of. Responding means switching contexts: reloading a different problem, a different repository and a different set of decisions. Two or three serious tasks a week was tiring in a familiar way. Working with many agents is tiring in a new way. My attention is spread across more problems, and I find moving between them much more mentally draining. What my GitHub history shows I pulled my GitHub contribution calendar for every month from January 2019 to today and marked my roles at Bold.org , which I joined in January 2020: Full Stack Engineer until August 2022, Principal Engineer until August 2025, and Vice President of Technology since then. These are GitHub’s contribution counts, including private work, so they mix commits, pull requests, reviews and issues. It is a rough signal of activity, not a measure of value. 2019 is an incomplete baseline: my job before Bold.org used a self-hosted GitLab, so GitHub only shows what I did outside it. But the shape is hard to ignore. The first part of the curve is what I expected: My busiest coding years at Bold.org were the early ones. 2020 was my highest year, with 2,711 contributions. 2021 dropped to 1,839 and 2022 to 1,498. The Principal Engineer years were flat and lower. From August 2022 to July 2025 I averaged 114 contributions a month, against 173 as a Full Stack Engineer. My lowest year was 2023, with 1,189. The first months as VP of Technology looked the same. From August to December 2025 I averaged 111 a month, and December 2025 was my quietest month since joining Bold.org, with 50. As a Principal Engineer, more of my work went into architecture, deep dives into concepts, setting up projects and planning, rather than fixing bugs or iterating on features. Becoming VP of Technology continued that shift, with even less feature work expected. At least until AI came along. Then 2026 happened: I am back at my Full Stack Engineer pace. By October 27 I am at 2,102 contributions, already more than any full year from 2021 to 2025. Over the same period in 2020 I had 2,371, so 2026 is close to my busiest year but not above it. August 2026 is the busiest month in the whole timeline. 427 contributions, against a previous high of 319 in April 2020. My normal day moved back up. The median weekday was 3 or 4 contributions every year from 2022 to 2025. In 2026 it is 7, close to the 8 I had in 2020. Fewer weekdays without GitHub activity. Through October 27, I had 18 weekdays with zero contributions, compared with 40–46 across each full year from 2022 to 2025. These are days without recorded GitHub activity, not days off work. Heavy days became routine again. From 2022 to 2025 I had exactly one day per year with 24 or more contributions. In 2026 I already have 16, almost the 17 I had in all of 2020. Almost all of this is private work. The dashed line in the chart is public contributions only: it was near zero from 2021 to 2025 and came back this year, with 191 so far, but that is still less than a tenth of 2026. The twist is the role. In 2020 I was a full-stack engineer doing feature work full time, and this is roughly what that looked like on GitHub. Today I lead engineering at Bold.org and do far less feature work than I used to. On paper my graph should look like my Principal Engineer years, or lower. Instead it is back where it was when writing code was my whole job. What changed is how much work feels worth taking on. When coding is cheap, I can fix bugs I would previously have left alone, improve patterns across the codebase, take on new projects and turn more ideas into something real. Much of this is work I would never have considered before. Agents did not just make my existing workload faster to finish. They made it easy to give myself a much bigger one. Bursts, then burnout Looking at the monthly totals, 2026 is not one steady climb. It is a series of bursts. January and February were the first clear burst, with 277 and 233 contributions. This is when I started working seriously with agents, and when the observability experiment that became our internal company agent took off. Every week revealed something new I could suddenly delegate, and I wanted to try all of it. March to June generally winds down, from 203 contributions in March to 77 in June. But April was a smaller burst along the way, another month when I had ideas and acted on them. I think improvements in the models were part of that renewed energy. Its monthly total of 187 is below January to March, but it includes a 29-contribution day and 68 public contributions, my highest public total of the year. August is the biggest burst of all. Coming back from my summer break, the calendar shows a full week of zero contributions in early August. Then every weekday from August 10 to August 27 was between 14 and 43. August ended at 427 contributions, the busiest month in the whole timeline. September stayed high at 301. Every cycle starts the same way. A new model or a new workflow makes something possible that was not possible last month, and my head fills with ideas. Because implementation is now cheap, there is no natural friction stopping me from pursuing all of them at once. So I do. I start more agents, open more threads and say yes to more experiments. That works for a few weeks. Then the reviewing and context switching catch up with me, and I pull back to a more stable flow. I stay there until something exciting comes along, or until a holiday recharges me enough that I go straight back into another burst. I count three of these cycles since January. At the end of a burst, I feel tired of AI. I do not want to start another agent or think of more ideas. I do my normal work, but I stop chasing the extra projects and possibilities because I do not have the mental bandwidth for them. The low season is not low anymore The part that surprised me most is not the peaks. It is how much I am doing between them. March did not feel like the bursts in January, February or August, but I was still doing substantial work. It had 203 contributions, against my Principal Engineer average of 114 a month. I was still acting on ideas, but that level of activity no longer felt like an exceptional push. Even when I think I am taking it easy, there are still agent results to work through, reviews to finish and small things that are now “just a quick prompt”. June was genuinely low, with 77 contributions, comparable to my quieter Principal Engineer months. Maybe that was when all the tiredness caught up with me. Not every quiet month is higher than before. But outside the bursts, I still find myself taking on more work than I used to. That is what I mean by the low season not feeling low anymore. Where that leaves me AI made room for work I would never have considered before. I like being able to fix more things and turn more ideas into something real. But the capacity to implement those ideas has grown much faster than my capacity to think about them. Eventually I stop wanting to start another agent and go back to just doing my normal work. I have not figured out a balance. For now, I am noticing that being able to do more keeps turning into doing more. And I am tired. A note on how this article was written: AI helped me pull and analyze my GitHub contribution data, build the chart and draft this article. The experience, decisions and opinions are mine. © 2026 Orestis Ioannou LinkedIn GitHub Email RSS

title: Why I Am a Programmer
body_text: Alfie John > Why I am a programmer Why I am a programmer There they sit, the preschooler class encircling their mentor, the substitute teacher. "Now class, today we will talk about what you want to be when you grow up. Isn't that fun?" The teacher looks around and spots the child, silent, apart from the others and deep in thought. "Jonny, why don't you start?" she encourages him. Jonny looks around, confused, his train of thought disrupted. He collects himself, and stares at the teacher with a steady eye. "I want to code demos," he says, his words becoming stronger and more confidant as he speaks. "I want to write something that will change peoples perception of reality. I want them to walk away from the computer dazed, unsure of their footing and eyesight. I want to write something that will reach out of the screen and grab them, making heartbeats and breathing slow to almost a halt. I want to write something that, when it is finished, they are reluctant to leave, knowing that nothing they experience that day will be quite as real, as insightful, as good. I want to write demos." Silence. The class and the teacher stare at Jonny, stunned. It is the teachers turn to be confused. Jonny blushes, feeling that something more is required. "Either that or I want to be a fireman."   -- Denthor of ASPHYXIA (aka Grant Smith), TUT7.TXT (1993) In the Beginning... I grew up in a pre-mainstream Internet world. A time when only a handful of kids at my primary school had a computer. We lived in a rough neighbourhood and so having a computer meant that you were a target for robbery. As we all knew somebody who had their computer stolen at least once, having a computer was kept on the low down. But we still found each other. Each time word got out that some kid got a new computer, they was suspiciously quizzed before being let into our digital posse. A lot of my childhood was spend living indoors behind a buzzing 14" CRT, pirating games with other kids via 3.5" single-density floppies with their corners drilled out, and once in a while even playing them. But I was more of a collector than gamer. Like Ash from Pokemon - got to catch them all. And the people who created computer games were my idols. I was always in awe of what they could do with that big, heavy, beige box under the table. One day word spread that there was a way to edit saved game files via XTreeGold's Hex View that gave you unlimited lives and allowed you to skip stages. With each new game that came out, the race was on to see who could be the first to flip the right bits to get the powerups. It was seriously heart pumping. Although only tinkering, it felt like we were our own gods. We bought a modem a few years later and soon after got a copy of The Australian BBS Listing - a textfile containing most of the publically accessible BBSes online. I dialed every one of them (but that's for another blog post). It opened up a whole new world to explore. Instead of just a handful of kids pirating games via Sneakernet, I was connected to the digital underground - a world where anything digital was within reach (some even had Internet gateways). Even the newest blockbusters that I had only read about in PC Zone magazine were all there for me to leech. All of them, soon slowly trickling down the wire via ZMODEM. But there was something different with these BBS downloaded games. Not something bad, but something exciting. Each time these games were run, it was like a short commercial was played before the title screen. Now I'm not talking about commercials selling steak knives. Instead, these were brazen posters screaming fuck you by the people who had managed to crack the game's copy protection code and were now distributing the game illegally for free. I later found out that these commercials were called cracktros. The precursor to demos and what started the whole demoscene. But simply calling them demos just doesn't give them justice. They were more of an out of body experience. Sensory overload. Like what you would feel at 2am, half tipsy, half asleep and being woken up stunned as you stare at a late 90s acid hard trance film clip, feeling it inject directly into your cerebral cortex. Once it finished playing, you were frozen. Still unsure whether you saw something real or just imagined it all. The only thing you were sure of, was that it was awesome. Then one day while browsing the file section of some random BBS, I stumbed onto a file innocently called TUT1-9.ZIP. It's FILE_ID.DIZ caught my attention: +----------------------------+ | The ASPHYXIA VGA | | DEMO TRAINER SERIES! | | | | By Denthor of ASPHYXIA | | | | Documentation on how | | to code demo like effects | | in TP6/7! | | | |Full Pascal source included!| | | | From putting a pixel | | to sprites and animation | | to wireframe 3D to solid | | 3D! | | | | Get it now! | +----------------------------+ How to code demo like effects? You mean I too could be one of those sorcerers that had the computer under their complete control!? My heart raced as I added it to the download queue, fired up the aging Epsom LQ-300, then covered me ears as its loud ink needles hit the blue and white computer paper. I didn't know anything about programming but I was completely estatic with the potential. I followed along with Denthor's tutorials as much as I could, typed everything out and hoped that Borland's Turbo Pascal 6.0 wouldn't laugh at me too much. It only gave me a basic understanding of how all the pieces to the puzzle fit together, but it was enough to whet my appetite and crave for more. I wasn't even into my teens yet but I definitely knew at the time that I didn't want to watch demos or play computer games anymore. I wanted to make them. I wanted to be elite. I wanted to be a programmer. See the Hacker News discussion ! about me signal me email me

title: The Goose Programming Language
body_text: The Goose Programming Language · Goose Goose Docs Tutorial Reference Spec Library Samples Benchmarks GitHub The Goose Programming Language Why Goose Features One memory model: data stacks freed at scope exit Memory never moves, so references survive growth Safe references, no annotations Nested data stays inline Enums in two sizes Links narrower than pointers Saving and loading data as bytes In-place construction Returning errors across calls Generics and function blocks Threads with no shared memory Compiling to and calling C Where the speed comes from Limitations Install a release Build and run Documentation Status License Authors History & Use of AI The Goose Programming Language A memory-safe systems language with no heap allocator, garbage collector, or lifetime annotations. In this repository's benchmarks, Goose runs faster than C++ and Rust while using less memory. Tutorial · Reference · Specification · Command line · Packages · Samples · Benchmarks · Standard library Goose has syntax familiar to C and Rust programmers, but there is no heap . Every dynamic value lives inline on data stacks managed by the compiler. Growth advances a pointer, and memory is freed when its scope ends. The language's type and lifetime rules make this memory model safe to use. Why Goose Faster than C++ and than safe Rust, while memory safe. Over sixteen benchmarks Goose runs at 3.3x the speed of idiomatic C++, 1.16x hand-optimized C++ and 1.12x the best safe Rust, and uses 1.9x, 1.3x and 1.2x less memory ( results ). These gains come from Goose's data layouts and memory model. No allocator, no GC, no reference counting, no destructors. Memory is a handful of data stacks that the compiler assigns statically. Freeing a structure with a million elements takes a single store, no matter how deeply it is nested. Growth preserves references. A reference into a growing array stays valid for as long as the array does. In the corresponding benchmarks, Goose keeps typed references where C++ must call reserve and safe Rust uses u32 indices. Memory safe with zero annotations. There is no lifetime syntax, there are no aliasing or exclusivity rules, and there is no unsafe . The compiler infers what every reference is rooted at and rejects references that could outlive their owners. Nested data stays inline. A string, an array of strings, a record with variable-size fields and an array of those records are each stored as one contiguous block that contains no pointers. A example record that takes 160 bytes and one allocation in C++ takes 29 bytes and no allocations in Goose. Variable sized Enums. Variable-mode ADTs store each value at the size of its own variant rather than that of the largest variant. On the benchmark that exercises this, they use 4x less memory than a Rust enum and run at 2x its speed. Links narrower than pointers. A relative reference stores a typed, checked link as a 1, 2 or 4-byte offset. Structures built from them are position independent, so a data structure can be written to a file as is. Saving it is a single write, and loading it is a single read followed by a verification pass that rejects malformed or hostile data. Everything is built in place, guaranteed. A value is constructed at its final destination through any depth of calls. items.push(parse(line)) writes the parsed record directly into the array, and returning a growable array by value does not copy it. Returns across multiple calls. return err from load returns from a function any number of frames up the call stack. It is checked statically, and needs no unwinder, no Result type and no ? on every call. Threads with no shared memory. A worker is compiled as a separate program with its own memory, and flat values are passed between threads through typed queues with a memcpy . Data races, locks, atomics and memory orderings do not exist in the language. Generics and higher-order functions with no overhead. An untyped parameter is generic. Function values are compile-time entities, so xs.filter() { it > 0 } compiles to what the handwrittend loop would looks like and builds its result directly in its destination. Compiles to C and can call C. Goose compiles to one C file, so it runs wherever a C compiler does and calls C directly through extern fn . The bundled TinyCC backend compiles and runs a program in-process, with no build step. The tutorial walks through all of this by example, the reference covers the whole language topic by topic, the specification has the exact rules, and the benchmarks have the numbers, including the cases where Goose loses. Features This section focuses on what distinguishes Goose. The tutorial explains these features in more detail, and the samples show them in thirty-one complete programs. One memory model: data stacks freed at scope exit A program has the native call stack, static data and N data stacks, where the compiler works out N. A data stack is a large address-space reservation with a bump pointer, and there is no other memory. At most one resizable value is live per stack and it is always on top, so growth never moves anything and never checks a capacity. All of this is proved at compile time; the runtime tracks only the bump pointers. for round in 3 { var scratch : u8 [ >.. ] = [] ; // grow-only: growth is a pointer bump for i in 100000 { scratch . push ((i % 256 ) as ! u8 ) ; } print ( "round " , round , ": " , scratch . len , " bytes" ) ; } // the free: one store to the stack top Memory never moves, so references survive growth struct Item { id : i32 , weight : f32 } var items : Item [ >.. ] = [] ; let first .= items . push ( Item { 1 , 0.5 }) ; // a reference to element 0 for i : i32 in 2 .. 1000001 { items . push ( Item { i , 0.0 }) ; } first . weight = 99.5 ; // still valid, a million pushes later push returns a reference to the new element, so a program can link elements while building the array. A vector<T> or Vec<T> may reallocate and cannot provide this guarantee. Stable references account for several benchmark gains. Safe references, no annotations Every reference and slice has a static root : the variable that bounds its target's lifetime. A reference must not outlive the variable that owns its target or access that target through an incompatible type. The compiler infers roots and specializes functions for them, so no annotations are needed. There are no aliasing or exclusivity rules. When a lifetime check fails, the error names the reference's root and its destination: fn longest (a : u8 [ : ] , b : u8 [ : ]) -> u8 [ : ] { if a . len >= b . len { a } else { b } } var outer : u8 [ >.. ] = [] ; var w = outer[ .. ] ; { var inner : u8 [ >.. ] = [] ; format (inner , "inner text" ) ; w = longest (outer , inner) ; // error: storing a reference rooted at inner, } // which does not outlive the destination (§9.2) A slice T[:] lets a function accept a range from any array kind without copying its elements. For example, split returns slices into its input, and a dictionary keyed by u8[:] stores views of strings rather than copies. Nested data stays inline There is no single array type. Instead there is a family of array types that differ only in how their size can change. Every member is laid out as [metadata][elements...] , inline and packed, never as a pointer to a separate block of elements: Type What it is T[k] fixed size, known at compile time T[] , T[varint] sized at construction, frozen after; a fixed or variable-width length T[..k] , T[..] capacity inline; grows and shrinks within it T[>..] grow-only : the most commonly used kind; references into it stay valid T[>..<] grow-shrink : stacks, queues, heaps Strings are u8 arrays: u8[>..] is a builder, u8[] a finished string stored inline in whatever holds it, u8[..16] a small string inside a struct, u8[:] a view. A struct may contain variable-size parts, which are stored inline in declaration order, so a record is a sequence of bytes with no indirection in it: struct Item { sku : u8 [ varint ] , qty : varint , cents : varint } struct Order { id : varint , customer : u8 [ varint ] , items : Item [ varint ] } var book : Order [ >.. ] = [] ; book . push ( Order { id : 1001 , customer : "alice" , items : [ Item { sku : "SKU-441" , qty : 2 , cents : 1999 } , Item { sku : "SKU-7" , qty : 1 , cents : 500 }] }) ; That order is 29 bytes and 0 allocations . As C++ std::string + std::vector<Item> it is 160 bytes and 1 allocation, and as Rust String + Vec<Item> it is 153 bytes and 4 allocations. An entire order book is a single array, so reading it streams through the cache. The trade-off is that an array of variable-size elements is sequential: you can iterate it but not index it (unless you keep a second array of references into it as an index). Enums in two sizes Algebraic data types are the only form of dynamic polymorphism; there is no inheritance and there are no vtables. Every ADT can be stored in two ways, chosen at the point of use. Fixed mode ( Shape ) stores a tag plus room for the largest payload, so values can be indexed and overwritten. Variable mode ( Shape.. ) gives each value exactly the size of its variant. An array of such values becomes sequential and a value never changes variant, but in exchange you may take references into a payload: enum Shape { Circle { r : f64 } , Rect { w : f64 , h : f64 } , Dot } var packed : Shape .. [ >.. ] = [] ; // 9, 17 and 1 bytes, not 17 each packed . push ( Shape . Circle { r : 1.0 }) ; packed . push ( Shape . Rect { w : 2.0 , h : 3.0 }) ; packed . push ( Shape . Dot ) ; for s in packed { match s { Rect & r => { r . w += 1.0 ; } , _ => {} } // edits the payload in place, inside the array } Case functions provide another way to dispatch on a variant: define one overload per variant. Calls dispatch on the tag through a jump table, and the compiler checks that the overloads cover every variant: fn area (s : Shape . Circle ) -> f64 { 3.14159 * s . r * s . r } fn area (s : Shape . Rect ) -> f64 { s . w * s . h } fn area (s : Shape . Dot ) -> f64 { 0.0 } for s in packed { print (s , " area " , area (s)) ; } Links narrower than pointers A T& is a machine address: it takes eight bytes and never dangles. A relative reference is the same link stored as a narrow offset. A T&<u32> is measured from the field itself to a target in the same array, so the structure is position independent. A T&<u32 in pool> is measured from the base of a named pool, so other arrays can link into the pool. T&<u32>? uses offset 0 as null. Here is a binary search tree in one grow-only array, with 12-byte nodes: struct Node { key : i32 , left : Node &< u32 >?, right : Node &< u32 >? } // 12 bytes, links included fn insert (pool : Node [ >.. ] &, key : i32 ) { if pool . len == 0 { pool . push ( Node { key : key }) ; return ; } var cur .= pool[ 0 ] ; // .= binds a reference; = would copy the node loop { if key == cur . key { return ; } let next = if key < cur . key { cur . left } else { cur . right } ; if next { cur .= next ; continue ; } // narrowed by `if`: next is a Node& if key < cur . key { cur . left .= pool . push ( Node { key : key }) ; } else { cur . right .= pool . push ( Node { key : key }) ; } return ; } } References are transparent (there is no * or -> ). .= binds or retargets a reference, and Node? is a nullable reference that if , guard and assert narrow. The insert is one push and one store, and the push cannot invalidate cur . When lifetimes are not nested, a reusable pool pairs a grow-only array with a hidden freelist. alloc_ref reuses a free slot or pushes a new one, and free returns a slot to the pool. Since a slot's memory is never actually freed, a stale slot reads a different value of the correct type rather than corrupting memory. Saving and loading data as bytes var image : u8 [ >.. ] = tree . to_bytes () ; // a framed byte image of the whole array var loaded , ok = from_bytes < Node [ >.. ] > (image) ; // verified before it becomes a value image[image . len - 3 ] = 200 ; // tamper with a link ... var bad , bok = from_bytes < Node [ >.. ] > (image) ; // ... and it is false and an empty array The tree's links are self-relative, so the tree means the same thing wherever it is stored. Saving it writes its bytes and loading it reads them back, with no serializer, no schema and no pointer fixups. from_bytes checks the framing, every tag, every length and every link before the bytes become a value, so a corrupt or hostile file makes it return false , never a wild reference. In-place construction The copy-free construction guarantee ( spec §4.3 ) says a constructed value is always built at its final location, which is passed down through calls. A function returning a grow-only array by value writes its elements directly into the caller's variable, or into a field of the record being built inside another array, so out-parameters are rarely needed. words . push ( str ( "word" , i)) ; // formatted straight into the new element let evens = xs . filter () { it % 2 == 0 } ; // built straight into `evens`: no temporary book . push ( Order { id : 1001 , customer : "alice" , items : parse_items ( "SKU-441:2:1999;SKU-7:1:500" ) }) ; Returning errors across calls struct User { name : u8 [ .. 16 ] , age : i32 } fn load (text : u8 [ : ]) -> User [ >.. ] , u8 [] { var users : User [ >.. ] = [] ; each_split (text , ' \n ' ) { users . push ( parse_user (it)) ; } ; return users , "" ; } fn parse_user (line : u8 [ : ]) -> User { // returns a User: no Result, no error parameter let comma = find (line , "," ) ; guard comma >= 0 else { return [] , str ( "expected name,age: " , line) from load ; } let age , ok = parse_int (line[comma + 1 .. ]) ; guard ok else { return [] , str ( "bad age: " , line) from load ; } let name = trim (line[ .. comma]) ; return User { name : name , age : age as i32 } ; } return E from f returns E as the result of the innermost active call of f , however many frames up that call is. Every function in between keeps its plain signature. The construct is checked statically: every call of parse_user must lie inside a load call, so nothing can go uncaught at runtime. It is implemented as a hidden discriminant checked in each frame rather than as an unwinder, and the message is built directly where load 's caller wants it. The parsers in the samples use it for every syntax error. Generics and function blocks fn twice (x) { x + x } // an untyped parameter is a generic one fn each_pair < T , F > (xs : T [ : ]) { // F is a function value: a compile-time entity for i in 0 .. xs . len - 1 { F (xs[i] , xs[i + 1 ]) ; } } fn first_gap (xs : i64 [ : ]) -> i64 { each_pair (xs) { a , b => if b - a > 1 { return a ; } } ; // returns from first_gap, not each_pair return - 1 ; } let evens = xs . filter () { it % 2 == 0 } ; let total = fold (xs , 0 ) { acc , x => acc + x } ; sort (xs) { a , b => a > b } ; Everything is monomorphized. Type arguments are inferred from argument types; type parameters that do not appear in those types can be supplied explicitly. Function values are passed as generic parameters. Every call of a function value is direct and can be inlined, function values cannot escape, and there are no closure objects or function pointers, so a higher-order function compiles to exactly the loop it looks like. A block may return from its lexically enclosing function, and nested functions can use the enclosing function's locals. Threads with no shared memory thread_fn worker () { // a separate program with its own memory loop { let job = qget < Job > () ; // blocks on the typed queue for Job guard job . n >= 0 else { break ; } // -1 means stop qput ( Result { n : job . n , digits : count_digits (job . n) }) ; } } for i in n { ids . push ( thread_spawn (worker)) ; } There is no shared mutable memory. A thread_fn and everything it calls is compiled as its own program with its own data stacks and its own copies of the globals. Values are passed between threads through typed queues, one per type, and must be flat , with no references at any depth. Passing them is cheap because a flat Goose value is contiguous: a job or a result can carry real data, such as pixels, and passing it is a single memcpy . A failed check or abort in a worker started with thread_spawn_contained ends only that worker. Its message goes to whoever waits for it, not to stderr, so a supervisor can log it and start another: var why : u8 [ >.. ] = [] ; while ! thread_wait ( thread_spawn_contained (serve , attempt) , why) { log (why) ; // "assert failed (serve.goose:12)" why . clear () ; attempt ++; } The first thread_wait(id, msg) for a worker takes the message; a caller that doesn't ask for it loses it. Compiling to and calling C extern fn hypot (x : f64 , y : f64 ) -> f64 ; // straight from libm extern fn crc32_bytes (s : const u8 [ : ]) -> u32 ; // a slice crosses as { data, len } extern fn stats_of (xs : i32 [ : ] , out : Stats & ) ; // a struct filled through a pointer An extern fn binds a Goose signature to a C symbol. The math and os modules use this interface. Only types with supported C representations may cross the boundary; unsupported signatures are rejected at the declaration. The compiler emits one C file for the whole program. The bundled TinyCC backend can compile and run that C inside the Goose compiler's process. Where the speed comes from Much of the speed comes from the memory model: no heap allocation or per-object teardown, contiguous data, narrow links, and enums sized for the variant they contain. Every index is bounds-checked, and the compiler removes checks it can prove unnecessary. An assert on a slice length often lets the compiler remove the remaining checks in a kernel, so that the kernel can be vectorized. --bce-lines reports the checks that remain. checkfree fn rejects a kernel if any bounds check remains in it; index types let graph edges keep the validation done while the graph was built. Benchmark measurements use whole-process wall-clock time, including teardown. Geometric mean over 16 benchmarks vs idiomatic C++ vs hand-optimized C++ vs best safe Rust speed, MSVC backend 3.51x 1.24x 1.13x speed, clang backend 3.54x 1.26x 1.19x peak memory 1.95x less 1.32x less 1.25x less The summary explains the gains and losses; results.md has every measurement, and design.md explains what the suite tests. Limitations You have to think about where data lives: who owns it, and how long its scope lasts. Usually the owner is the function that builds the data, which needs no extra work; when it is not, the data goes in a reusable pool. Recursive functions cannot keep growable data across a recursive call. Scratch data must end before the call, and data that outlives the call is passed in as a pool. Arrays of variable-size elements can be iterated but not indexed (unless you keep an index of references beside them). A fixed-mode enum cannot be pointed into, and a variable-mode one cannot be overwritten. You make this choice per container. There are no escaping closures, no function pointers and no dynamic dispatch beyond ADT tags, and only whole-program compilation is supported. A slot that was returned to a reusable pool but is still referenced reads whatever its next owner put there. That is a logic bug, but never memory corruption. Tutorial §18 is the full list. Install a release Prebuilt compilers for Windows (x64), Linux (x64) and macOS (Apple silicon and Intel) are on the releases page , with the graphics, audio, ui and physics packages compiled in. Unpack one anywhere and put its directory on PATH: the compiler finds the standard library, TinyCC's runtime and the packages beside itself, and keeps what it builds under ~/.goose ( GOOSE_HOME ). The archive also holds these docs, the samples and the VS Code extension. Running a program in-process ( goose file.goose ) needs nothing else on Windows. On Linux it needs the C library's headers ( libc6-dev , or glibc-devel ); on macOS, the SDK of the Xcode command line tools ( xcode-select --install ). goose build also needs a C compiler: Visual Studio 2022 or later, or clang, on Windows; gcc or clang elsewhere. The Linux compiler needs glibc 2.35 or later (Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12), and the macOS compiler needs macOS 13.3 or later. macOS keeps a downloaded archive's files from running until xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine is run on the unpacked directory. Build and run You need CMake 3.27 or later, a C++20 compiler (MSVC, clang or gcc) and Python 3 for the test and sample runners. TinyCC, which the in-process backend is built from, is part of the tree. The graphics, audio, ui and physics modules are packages in repositories of their own ( goose_gfx and goose_physics ; docs/design/packages.md ). -DGOOSE_BUILTIN_LIBS=all fetches them with git at configure time, at the pinned tags, and compiles them into the compiler, so programs that use them run with nothing else installed. Without that option the compiler is built on its own, and the first time a program imports one of these packages, the package is built into ~/.goose , which needs git, cmake and a C compiler. git clone https://github.com/aardappel/goose cd goose cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE = Release -DGOOSE_BUILTIN_LIBS = all cmake --build build --config Release GOOSE_BUILTIN_LIBS can also name some of the packages ( physics , or gfx , which includes audio and ui too). On Linux, SDL needs the X11 or Wayland development packages ( third_party/SDL/docs/README-linux.md ); without them the build leaves the gfx module out and says what to install. The runner scripts prefer build/Release , then build/RelWithDebInfo , then build , then build/Debug . Pass --exe to select a specific compiler; use an explicit Debug executable when testing with compiler assertions enabled. The compiler is build/goose ( build/Release/goose.exe with the Visual Studio generator), and it finds the standard library in the source tree it was built from. On Windows 10 version 1903 and later, its embedded manifest selects a UTF-8 process code page so compiler paths do not depend on the system locale. Earlier Windows versions retain their legacy code page. Generated native executables retain their own process settings. Run a program directly from source, in-process, with no C compiler and no build step ( goose run is the explicit form of the same command): build/goose samples/01_tour.goose Or build an executable, which is written beside the source. The compiler finds a C compiler on the machine ( goose toolchain shows which one) and links the generated C with the runtime and any native modules the program uses, including graphics. Programs that use threads must be built this way, since TinyCC cannot place thread-local storage. build/goose build samples/01_tour.goose && samples/01_tour build/goose build samples/27_gfx_cube.goose && samples/27_gfx_cube goose check only typechecks. --debug turns on the overflow, range and tag checks, each of which names its source line when it fails, and --bce-lines reports the bounds checks that remain on each line. Every resizable value lives on a data stack of 2 GB of reserved address space, committed as it is used, and --stack-reserve 16G changes that size. The command line describes every command and option, including how to write the C for a build system or a C host of your own ( goose -o tour.c tour.goose ). A program with C of its own lists that C in a sidecar file beside the source, foo.build beside foo.goose : c_sources = ["impl.c"]; . Both forms build that C, so an extern fn can call it either way. A program uses a library by writing import name from "source"; in its root file. The source is a directory ( "./lib" ), or a git repository at a tag or commit ( "owner/repo@v1" on GitHub, "host/owner/repo@ref" ), which is fetched into ~/.goose and built there once per C compiler ( packages ). A program using audio plays procedural mono/stereo PCM through SDL3 without opening a graphics window. See the audio reference . The test suite and the samples run on Windows, macOS and Linux: python test/run_tests.py python samples/run_samples.py For editing, the VS Code extension gives syntax highlighting, the compiler's language server ( goose lsp : errors as you type, hover, go to definition, completion, rename, symbols) and one-key runs through the JIT: code --install-extension vscode/goose-language.vsix Other editors can run goose lsp themselves; editors has the configuration for Neovim, Helix and Emacs. Documentation Documentation index : the map of everything below, and the root of the documentation site built from these files ( how ). Tutorial : the friendly introduction, by example. Read this first. Language reference : every feature, topic by topic, with a compiling example for each. It covers the whole language and is written to be read. Language specification : the exact rules, when you want to know why something did not compile. Samples : thirty-one complete programs in reading order, from a tour of the language to a JSON parser, a threaded Mandelbrot, a file tree built from two pools, a spinning cube on the GPU, thousands of boxes raining into a heap and a to-do list in windows of widgets. Standard library : fourteen modules, all written in readable Goose under stdlib/ . They include gfx for graphics on SDL3's GPU API ( how it is built ) and physics for rigid body physics on Box3D ( how it is built ). The ui module provides fonts, text rendering and game HUDs . It also provides windows and widgets on Nuklear, drawn through gfx ( how it is built ). The command line : every command and option of goose , from running and building to writing the C yourself, the formatter and the language server. Building programs and using packages : libraries from git repositories or directories, a program's own C, and how to make a package of your own. Benchmarks : the numbers, with the full results and the design behind them. Implementation notes : how the compiler works, pass by pass, and how it is tested . Status Goose is new. What exists today is a whole-program compiler of about thirty thousand lines of C++, the specification, the standard library, the samples, and a test suite that CI runs on Windows, macOS and Linux with an extra sanitizer job. These are deliberately out of scope for now: moves for resizable values, more than one resizable per struct, labeled break , namespace privacy, and more OS/library access. Open items are tracked in the specification's Appendix B . License Goose is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0 . Authors Wouter van Oortmerssen : Language Design, Compiler Design, Coding standards. home page, twitter . Claude Fable : Compiler implementation, Benchmarking, Sample & Doc writing. History & Use of AI This repo was produced almost entirely with AI, from a human language design. I had designed Goose several years ago, and had started to implement it, but running a game startup (which is built on another programming language of mine, Lobster ) there was no time to finish it. Which was sad, because I knew Goose could do things other languages can't, and it should exist. I had not expected AI to help with this until Fable came out. I thought it might be capable enough to do a good job. I made it essentially clone the style and structure of my other recent compiler (Lobster), which is why if you look at the code, it looks rather similar to that. My initial design had left lots of things unspecified, and lots of back and forth with Fable made me decide on all of those, and it is now a better language for it. It is also an experiment in using AI to implement a new language, rather than reproduce an existing one. You may wonder why I had it work in C++, if clearly I could have used any language, like Rust, or my own Lobster, or.. Goose itself (that may still happen). With Fable, it was my observation that it is almost equally capable in any language, and the strong guardrails of Rust or other languages are not as pressing as they once were. Since the compiler emits C, you likely already need to have a C/C++ compiler around, so sticking inside one ecosystem would seem to simplify deployment and adoption. I've also integrated libtcc and who knows what other C libraries in the future. And, like I said, to have the compiler code mimic my existing Lobster compiler seemed fun, at least I can read it like it is my own. Built from README.md .

title: Cerebras Deploys Trillion-Parameter AI Models
body_text: How Cerebras Deploys Trillion-Parameter AI Models Skip to main content Products Customers Partners Developers Resources Pricing Company Contact us Get Started Oracle Cloud Infrastructure plans to offer Cerebras inference to AI labs, enterprises, and developers. Read more >> Oct 22 2026 How we deploy Trillion-parameter frontier models on Cerebras Sarah Chieng One of the most frequently asked questions we get is how we deploy large models on Cerebras wafer-scale chips. A single Cerebras WSE-3T wafer has 44 GB of on-chip memory, and trillion-parameter frontier models need terabytes for their weights alone. In this post, we’ll explain how we split a large frontier model across multiple WSE-3T wafers, to run multi-trillion parameter models at 1000-2000+ tokens per second. We’ll use the open source model Kimi K3, with ~3 trillion parameters, as an illustrative example. By the end, you'll understand: How we fit the full model into on-chip memory How we map the model across multiple chips How we handle a high # of concurrent requests Breaking it down with Kimi K3 Kimi K3 is an open source, 3T parameter model with 69 linear-attention layers and 24 dense layers. It scores an impressive 88.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (vs. GPT-5.6 Sol's 88.8%) and 91.2% on BrowseComp (vs. GPT-5.6 Sol's 90.4%). These results demonstrate frontier-level coding and agentic capabilities, even outperforming leading proprietary models on some benchmarks. Read more about Kimi K3 here . For this illustrative example, we use: A 256k assumed average request size 4-bit weight quantization (like the Hugging Face implementation ) An 8-bit KV cache #1: Size of Each layer To calculate the total number of Cerebras WSE-3T wafers we need to support Kimi K3, let’s first calculate the size of each model layer. Kimi K3 has 3 trillion parameters. If all 3T parameters are stored at 4 bits each, the raw parameter payload is: Dividing that payload by 93 layers then gives: #2: Number of Wafers Now that we know each layer needs about 16 GB, we can figure out how many layers fit on each 44 GB wafer. The answer depends on the layer type: Dense layers need additional room for a KV cache, because each dense (full-attention) layer stores the keys and values for every token in every active request. So, we place one dense layer per wafer and leave the remaining SRAM for its KV cache. Linear-attention layers do not require additional room for a KV cache. Instead of storing keys and values for every token, a linear-attention layer keeps a small, fixed-size state per request, regardless of context length. That leaves room for two linear layers per wafer (2 × 16 GB = 32 GB). Therefore, with Kimi K3’s 69 linear layers and 24 dense layers , we get: This gives us a total wafer count of 35 + 24 = 59 wafers. #3: Connecting the wafers together Cerebras executes models in a pipeline. After the Cerebras compiler maps the model layers across regions of wafers, the runtime maps the path for tokens to flow between wafers. For ultrafast latency, only activations need to be passed between the wafers, and this can be done via RDMA over Ethernet. This is roughly 2 microseconds per hop. It’s important to emphasize that because each Cerebras wafer has 44 GB of on-chip SRAM and each layer is only 16 GB, we are typically able to fit entire layers of the model directly on the chip. This means that in most cases, the model weights never have to move, and layers don’t need to be split across wafers. Only activations cross from one wafer to the next. #4: How we serve 1 request Now that we have our wafers connected together and the model laid out, we can think of each wafer as one stage in an assembly line: the model’s weights for each stage stay in place, and the request’s intermediate results move through the layer stages. For example, Wafer 1 runs model layers 1–2 and sends its activations to wafer 2. Wafer 2 runs layers 3–4 and passes its results to Wafer 3, and so on until the last wafer produces the next token. #5: How we serve many requests This raises a common misconception. If a token has to travel through each wafer in order, doesn’t each wafer sit idle while it waits for its turn? In effect, wouldn't the system be running at a batch size of one? No! If we only sent one request down the line at a time and waited for it to complete before starting the next request, this would be an inefficient use of the pipeline. Instead, we keep the entire pipeline full with different requests. Because the model is split into pipeline stages already, each stage can work on a different request at the same time. While stage 3 processes a token for request A, stage 2 processes one for request B, and stage 1 one for request C. In our example, each stage is a layer. In production, Cerebras uses much finer-grained stages, and many more of them. Loading player... Each stage can also process a micro-batch , a small group of requests, rather than a single request. So the number of requests in flight is roughly the number of stages times the micro-batch size. Loading player... To understand the tradeoff, smaller micro-batches make each request even faster, while larger micro-batches increase total throughput. #6: How many requests can we serve? The amount of on-chip memory allocated to KV cache determines the maximum number of concurrent requests. Every request in flight needs its own KV cache on each dense-layer wafer, so the size of on-chip memory sets the ceiling on concurrent requests. As explained above, we only need to calculate KV cache requirements for dense layers. For each 44 GB wafer that already has one dense layer, we can calculate the remaining space for the KV cache with: Total wafer storage - size of one dense layer. In this case: Calculating the # of Concurrent Requests To find the number of concurrent requests supported for any particular model mapping, we first calculate how much cache a single 256k request takes up: To then calculate the total number of concurrent requests this configuration would support, we divide: The total number of concurrent requests represents the number of simultaneous requests moving through the pipeline at any point in time. Unlike a GPU batch, those requests don’t wait for one another to finish, they stream through the pipeline continuously. Of course, neither concurrency nor batch size tells you exactly how efficiently an inference system performs. When evaluating the throughput of an inference system, the more meaningful metric is total token throughput per unit of power (e.g. tokens per second per megawatt), when measured at the same output generation speed. How this scales beyond 3T parameters The same approach extends to larger models: calculate the memory needed for weights and request state, distribute the model across wafers, and connect them into a pipeline. Each additional wafer contributes compute and on-chip memory, allowing us to accommodate models that exceed the capacity of any single chip. Thanks for learning with us! Interested in deploying a model on Cerebras or building with our inference cloud?
